## ══ STATUS (2026-10-25, latest) — F15 landed: a regex known at compile time ══

**F15 is the third family ported**, as the branch wrote it (B51, B52 and
B69). Every static regex is now checked at compile time (SB5023):
`sub`/`gsub`/`match`/`matchall` operands, every sed edit in every form, `=~`
under `&&`/`||`/`!`, and every dispatch arm. A dynamic pattern that fails to
compile now makes `sub`/`gsub` exit 2, as the other regex consumers
already did. The parser's first-edit check is gone. It ran as a parse
error, so it hid validate's other errors; they now appear alongside SB5023. The
specs are 39.36–39.56 (regex.sh), and DD#39 has an addendum. Journal 534.

**Backlog.** The sed-extent family (B62–B65, B67, B68) was never fixed on
the branch, so it is `bug-sed-expansion-extent`. Seven more tasks were filed
alongside it. The P1 among them is `bug-subscript-key-check-skips-positions`:
a word index ICEs natively and silently reads index 0 in C.

**Gates.** `mk test` 225/27/20; the sweep is 9525 = 9512 passing + 13 skips,
with 42 first-ever ids and no flips; the hook passes without bypass.

**Next: D1** (B113, a whole-int `[[ ]]` operand → SB4030), when DG says
go. The P1 above is offered ahead of it.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-24) — F14 landed: a `$` that names nothing ══

**F14 is the second family ported**, as the branch wrote it (B70, B39,
B66). In arithmetic, a `$` that starts no variable is SB4035 "stray `$`"
(base read the variable with the empty name, so `$(( $ + 1 ))` printed
1), and a nested `$(` or `$((` is SB4035 "is not an arithmetic operand".
`${}` and `${:…}` are SB4047 "names no variable" (base expanded the empty
name, and `${:0:1}` was a native ICE). An explicit index that fails to
parse reports its own error, not SB4041's advice to write the form the
author had already written. SB4032's unsupported-flag message loses three
runs of eighteen spaces. Journal 533.

**Five specs change code; their programs do not:** 31.46, 31.85 and
cov.356 (SB4020 to SB4035, "is not an arithmetic operand"), 31.67 (SB4020
to SB4035, "stray `$`") and 75.164 (SB4041 to SB4035). The DD#65, DD#72
and DD#80 addenda state the rules, among them the DD#80 addendum that
75.164 cited before it existed.

**B38 was never fixed on the branch**, though Step 0 recorded it so: base,
the branch and F14 agree on every one of its shapes. Under DG's rule it
became backlog, with B40 and B41: seven tasks in all. Among them is
`bug-echo-partial-line-before-abort`: with `x` empty, `echo "[${x:?m}]"`
prints `[` before it aborts, in both backends.

**Gates.** 19 new dual-mode specs, every one failing on base, and five
reversion runs, each turning red the specs that pin what it reverts.
Sweep: **9483 = 9470 passing + 13 skips**, 38 first-ever ids, no flips,
no retirements; `mk test` 226/27/20. Hunk ledger: 202 pending, 64
superseded, 62 ported, 1 reimplemented, 1 proposed drop.

**Next: F15**, regex and sed operands (B69, B51, B52, and the sed family
B62-B65/B67/B68 as one chain grammar), opening with its discussion.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-24) — F13 landed: re-lexed positions; SB4044 decided once ══

**F13 is the first family ported.** The branch's lexer origins and
`stmt_span` port as written (B3, B61, B54). A statement inside a quoted
capture, an index or a sed field now reports its own line and column; a
sub-scanner's fatal is no longer dropped (base silently miscompiled
`$'\101'` in a sed field); and transform diagnostics no longer report
1:1. Journal 532.

**SB4044 is decided by validate alone**, the refinement DG approved. It
runs first in the semantic batch, after binding resolution, over every
channel that binds a name, and `VersionState::define`'s spanless
backstop is now an ICE. That reverses half of journal 204's fork C, under
the 2026-10-04 rule that an ICE is a regression guard. Making it safe
fixed four bugs found on both binaries (B116-B119): a write before the
declaration compiled; merge phis, the function template and the
suppressed int tail specialization bound a const twice (false SB4044s);
one function's const blocked another's local; and `__forglob` clobbered
a source global and broke nested glob loops. B58, F5's capture cycle,
lands here too.

**DG's rule for the whole port:** behaviours that are not obviously bugs
stay unchanged, and questions and uncovered cases become backlog tasks.
F13 filed nine, among them `spec-harness-hides-compiler-ice`: the spec
harness keeps none of an ICE's text in `$err`.

**Gates.** 56 new dual-mode specs, every one failing on base, and 24
reversion stubs, each turning red only its own specs. Final sweep:
**9445 = 9432 passing + 13 skips**, no flips, no retirements; `mk test`
226/27/20. The commit hook's complexity gate caught `lower_function_stmt`,
a base violator the template change touched; its arity-defect loop is now
`report_arity_defects`, and the sweep was re-run. Hunk ledger: 216
pending, 64 superseded, 48 ported, 1 reimplemented, 1 proposed drop.

**Next: F14**, malformed names and arithmetic (B70, B39, B66), opening
with its discussion.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-24) — porting batch 531; Step 0 done ══

**Batch 531 becomes a port, not a merge.** Classifying the last 46 cold
lines stopped on real bugs, and their fixes grew into a context-sensitive
taint walker before DG stopped it. That work is held as `e98fca8` on the
local, unpushed branch `taint-walker-redesign`: 44 files, +5555/-2404,
101 new dual-mode specs. DG asked for a port to `hand-parser` one family
at a time, each opening with a discussion and his decision. The walker
itself is not ported. Journal 531.

**Taint is settled per body (T1-T3).** An attest lives in the body whose
command produced the taint, and no other body can attest it. Unattested
external output reaching a function's stdout taints `$(f)` (T1). A body
may not leave its own taint on a global or slot (T2, SB5067), and cannot
attest taint it received (T3, SB5088). Each body is checked once and
summarised, bottom-up; the W track implements it. Separately, a
whole-int `[[ ]]` operand becomes SB4030 (D1).

**Step 0 changed no behaviour.** Re-baseline at `1309385`: **9333 = 9320
passing + 13 skips**, the 202 branch-only ids retired, 0 first-ever and
exactly the 30 predicted fail-to-pass flips (block 6286459-6295791).
Every one of the branch's 330 hunks is in
`notes/tasks/batch-531-hunks.tsv`: 265 pending, 64 superseded walker
hunks, 1 proposed drop. All 127 findings were re-probed on both binaries
in both backends; `notes/tasks/batch-531-findings.md` indexes them by
the step that lands them.

**Next: F13**, positions in re-lexed text, opening with its discussion.
The coverage cohort (type check 14, validate 32) resumes after the
port's wrap-up, with a fresh union.

nested argument captures, redirected captures and suppressed tail

capture's blocks, silently ignoring its failure. A shared

specialization, keeping the first iteration checked and the stack constant.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-18) — owned streaming readers; 82 cold lines remain ══

**Nested readers no longer replace an outer pipeline's input.** Each site
owns its fd and pending producers in both backends. Following DG's
direction, consumption runs concurrently; completion closes the read end
before waiting and evaluating producer status. This fixes both silent
outer-record loss and pipe-capacity deadlocks. Parent stdin and loop
mutations retain their existing meaning. DD#122 and journal 527.

**Reader binding is lexical, not a post-SSA scan.** Calls, anonymous
captures, redirected commands and background children suspend the enclosing
pipe binding. A shared CFG pass closes/reaps exited regions, inner first,
including nonlocal loop/function transfers. END and abort preserve their
triggering status; authored waits retain reaped producer statuses for later
pipeline completion. DD#55's suppression/negation rules remain unchanged.
No forced producer termination or timeout was added.

**Redirect setup and cold contracts are repaired.** Command redirects
attach to the command block, not argument-setup assignments. C no longer
returns a null pointer for a missing collection slot. Shared loop-phi
updates and direct API assertions pin the source-inaccessible contracts;
obsolete singleton/message/wrapper answers are removed.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-17) — native instruction handlers: 9 → 0 ══

**DG chose close and wait, not forced termination.** Both backends now check
pipe/fork results before using outputs or recording pids. Construction failure
closes successful pipes and waits for started stages, retrying EINTR, with no
kill or kill timeout. Child pipe wiring and redirects share checked setup;
failed setup never runs the stage body. Pipeline echo retains write failure,
and explicit `3<>file` binds the correct descriptor. Journal 518; DD#55.

**Failed construction is not EOF.** Capturing pipelines skip their entire
consumer through a real SSA branch/phi join. Ordinary and capturing pipelines
share the stage builder, preserving suppressed/negated function stages. Actual
empty/short reads replace the target array instead of retaining old cells.

**FLAG and EXIT are distinct at delivery.** Separate runtime atomics prevent
FLAG from requesting shutdown; EXIT works without END. Both backends use
canonical END-region membership and loop/function checkpoints. Checkpoint
instructions are installed after two-pass discovery, which otherwise erased
them. FLAG-only programs receive none. DD#56 describes the corrected protocol.

cold production lines; C emitter **25 → 21**. No other file gains cold lines.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-15) — the type checker did the proof ══

**Historical method/classification claims below are corrected by journal 511
and the 2026-10-16 section above.**

**DG chose C, and it went further than the task filed.** 25 of the 27
functions in `parse/parser.rs` returning `Result<Option<Statement>, _>` now
return `Result<Statement, _>`. All **eight** cold lines are gone — 40% of the
file's cold cohort — **deleted, not ICE'd**, because the type now says what the
`unreachable!()` would have said. Among them the third unreachable user-facing
diagnostic (`return_producer_error` at `parse_return`). Net −24 lines. New
private `parse_statement_here` = "parse a statement the caller has already
established is there"; `parse_statement` is now a four-line wrapper doing the
EOF check and `.map(Some)`.

**The method is the finding.** The task said the other seven lines needed three
separate reachability probes first, since a cold line is a hypothesis. Wrong
instrument: **narrowing a signature is self-proving.** If a relay could carry a
live `None` the narrowed function does not typecheck and `rustc` names the
line — so the experiment and the fix are one edit, and the result is a proof
over every path, not one probe's corroboration. The compiler accepted all 25
and the two I left alone are *exactly* the two with a live `None`
(`parse_statement`, the real producer; `parse_list_operand`, whose `at_eof`
arm becomes SB4056 for a dangling `&&`). It partitioned the cohort without
being told which was which. Generalised in AGENTS.md: **when a cold line is a
type's fault, change the type and let the compiler enumerate.**

This also disposes of `parse_brace_else`'s `unreachable!()` from 509 — the one
ICE here that could never be unit-tested (reaching it required editing
`parse_if`), so under option A that line was cold *permanently*, outside the
spec ∪ unit-test union that defines the 100% target. It is now not a line.

**A message is not a site either.** `return_producer_error` has two call sites
raising byte-identical SB4014 text; `fn f() { return - }` produces the sentence
and fires the *warm* one. AGENTS.md's rule covered codes; it now covers
shared-constructor messages too — the test is the constructor's call-site
count, not the string's uniqueness.

**The gate caught a free rider, and it was hiding a compiler crash.** The
commit tripped the complexity gate on `parse_attest` — a pre-existing violator
(cc 12 / cog 6) that a *two-token* edit made visible, which is
grandfather-on-modify working as designed. Extracted `parse_attest_predicate`;
12/6 → 7/3. But I left it answering `Option<Expr>`, and the next coverage run
called it: `parser.rs` went 20 → **11** cold lines with one of the 11 *new* —
my own `Ok(None)`.

**Probing it found a bug.** `attest x in a` with no predicate (and the
two-binder map spelling) **ICEs the compiler**: `classify_attest` answers
`None`, `check_attest_form` silently returns, and `handle_attest_stmt` hits
`unreachable!("`attest` shape is fixed by parse_attest before lowering
(SB4014)")` — **an ICE naming a guarantee the parser did not provide.** The
scalar path is guarded by the predicate peek; the attest-all lead is reached
exactly when that peek fails, so nothing after `in ARRAY` required a predicate.
Pre-existing since the form existed; no spec had ever written one. Fixed where
the ICE says it is fixed — `parse_attest_predicate` returns `Result<Expr, _>`
and raises SB4014. Specs `93.59`/`93.60` + `93.61` positive control.

The sequence is the lesson: a cold line I created by hand, in a refactor whose
whole subject was cold lines, was a real bug — caught because I re-measured
instead of assuming. Predicted "8 gone"; measured "9 gone, 1 new", and the
discrepancy *was* the finding.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-14) — three diagnostics the suite had never read ══

**A new axis on the coverage queue: intersect cold lines with SB raise sites.**
Ranking by function finds clusters; this finds *lies*. A cold walker arm needs
a probe before you know what it is, but a cold `parse_error(.., "SB4014", ..)`
labels itself — someone thought a user could reach it. **277 raise sites, 148
codes, 56 with more than one site, 3 cold.** One of each kind. Journal 509; the
`GLOB` query is in AGENTS.md.

**One was a real gap.** `expect_rparen` (`expr.rs:1782`) has exactly one caller,
`parse_slurp_form` — the `$(<file)` form — and nothing in the suite had ever
written a malformed one. `sl.14` now does. It asserts the **message text**, not
the code: SB4014 is raised at ten places in `parse/`, so `$err == *SB4014*`
would pass if any of them fired. `"expected ')'"` is unique to this site.

**Two were lies about the language**, both now `unreachable!()`.
`parser.rs:705` converted a `parse_if` `None` into `SB4027 "expected \`if\`"`,
but `parse_if` cannot return `Ok(None)` — every arm is an `Err` or ends in
`Ok(Some(make_if(..)))`. `parser.rs:3384` raised `SB4014 "expected redirect
operator"` after all three callers had already gated on the token set. Same
shape as DG's `len @a` ruling: an unreachable arm handling a rejected spelling
documents the spelling as supported.

**Both pass the rival test, and for an unusual reason** — the guard and the ICE
are about *different functions*. `matches!(peek, Tok::If)` is a claim about the
token stream; the ICE is a claim about `parse_if`'s contract, which the peek
structurally cannot check. `parse_redirect`'s asserts that three separate
callers still gate, and no one gate can speak for the other two. Only
`parse_redirect` is unit-testable (direct call, contract deliberately broken);
`parse_brace_else` is the "do not chase" category.

**The `parse_if` signature, reframed** (DG chose **C**; see the 10-15 section). The commit message
said the 27 functions sharing `Result<Option<Statement>, _>` do so as a
"None = not my form" dispatch protocol. **That is wrong and the journal
corrects it.** `dispatch_statement` is a total match on the head token; every
arm commits and nothing backtracks. The `None` means only "there is no
statement here", it originates solely at `parse_statement:270` (EOF /
comment-only), and three functions relay it. **So 23 of the 27 can never return
`None`** — the `Option` is repetition, not protocol, and `parse_brace_else` was
just the one place that answered the impossible case with a user-facing
diagnostic instead of ignoring it.

Three-way fork, DG's call: **A** leave it (committed — one `unreachable!()`,
zero churn); **B** narrow `parse_if` alone (deletes the cold line, makes 1 of
27 odd, `.map(Some)` at `dispatch_statement:298` — worst of both); **C** narrow
all 23 (removes the class, not the instance; `parse_statement` and
`dispatch_statement` keep their `Option`; touches 23 signatures and their call
sites). My earlier "breaking a 27-function convention" overstated B and C — the
only honest objection to C is its size.

Sweep **8377** (predicted 8375 + 2 before running), zero failures, zero flips,
two new ids both `sl.14`, liveness 258. `mk test` 125 + 27 + 20.

**Ran journal 507's census over the rest of the compiler.** Four more rules
raised by live code and named only in spec comments: **SB4017, SB4021, SB4023,
SB4024**. Unlike SB5027 these were not masked — each is the sole diagnostic for
its program; there was simply nothing asserting them. Added `csfx.1`-`csfx.3`
(the compound-suffix family) and `0.5q` (bare-`return` spelling of SB4017),
and tightened `55.13`/`55.14` to name SB4016/SB4017. Journal 508.

**The census pattern was wrong twice before it was right.** Scanning for the
code as a quoted literal misses the **17 of 153** codes interpolated into a
hand-rolled `format!("…[SB5055]…")` — the same format-string blind spot
AGENTS.md records for message text. Matching anywhere then counts `#`-comment
mentions on the spec side as assertions. **Filter comments on both sides, and
run both directions**; `comm -13` is what found the blind spot. Corrected
pattern is in AGENTS.md.

**Two stale cross-references.** `check_subscript_index`'s doc named
"(SB4042, type_check)" — DD#80 *deferred* SB4042, so none has ever existed; the
real rule is SB4030, verified live. And `rdr.47`'s comment said a backgrounded
compound is SB4022; it is SB4024.

**The reversion proof caught a rival again.** Stubbing all four turned **six**
specs red against a predicted five — the sixth was `55.14`, already SB4017's
positive but asserting only `-n $err`. My `0.5p` was a verbatim duplicate of
it. **Before writing a positive, stub the rule and see what already fails.**

**Not a flake — a latent spec bug, found via the xtrace.** `c:cli.31/32/40/41/42`
flipped passing→failing in one sweep and back in the next. I wrote it up as
unexplained and filed a task claiming `chk` discards failure evidence. **Both
wrong.** DG asked "what about the xtrace?" — `common.sh`'s `setup()` has always
redirected each spec file into `spec/.trace/$(date +%a)/<file>.<mode>` under
`set -x` (`exec 3>&1` is why `chk` writes to fd 3), and the failing block was
still there, timestamped to match `spec.db`.

It held the answer verbatim: `mktemp -d` returned `/tmp/tmp.nkqYLkSBp3`, and
all five assert `$(grep -c SB f) = 0` against messages that echo the
`--sysroot` path. **The grep counted the directory name.** That explains c-mode
only (each file *and mode* gets its own dir), all five together (one dir),
never reproducible (fresh name), once in 400+ (~0.2% = 9 positions × 1/62²).
Fixed to `grep -cE 'SB[0-9]{4}'`, reproduced deterministically before and
after. Blast radius was exactly those five — every other such grep already
names a complete code. Task closed as filed on a false premise.

**Two lessons in AGENTS.md:** read the trace before theorising, and an
assertion must not be able to match the scaffolding — a bare `SB` against text
embedding a `mktemp` path renders identically to a real regression.

Gates: sweep **8375** exactly as predicted (+4 ids × 2 modes), zero failures,
zero flips, zero new-id surprises on the re-run; `mk test` 124 + 27 + 20.

regression this is all about was unguarded at the site I had declared safe.

**The fix was not a second test.** Two sites making one claim became one
function: `types::var_slot(vars, key) -> VarSlot`. One ICE line, one sentence,
one test — and it protects both callers because both route through it.

It is a map lookup. `codegen/test_support.rs` (yesterday's `with_builder`
harness, built specifically to reach the guard behind the builder borrow)
became unused and was **deleted**. Scaffolding that exists only to reach
duplicated logic is a sign the logic should not be duplicated.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-12) — two passes that disagreed about what a function is ══

**Ranking cold lines turned up two P1 bugs, one of them a silent wrong
answer.** The coverage queue's head was `build_function_pipeline_stage`; four
of its five cold lines are the DD#116 recursion backstop (category 2, still
owed a unit test), but the fifth was a `?` on `state.function_bodies` whose
*caller* guards on `state.known_functions`. Journal 498.

**Those two sets disagree by design.** `known_functions` is a whole-program
pre-pass (`entry.rs:16`); `function_bodies` is filled when the `fn` statement
is *lowered* (`statements.rs:151`). A function called before its definition is
in the first and not the second — so the `?` was a silent fall-through to
"treat it as an external command."

- `echo hi | up` before `fn up { … }` compiled clean and died at **runtime**
  with the runtime's own `sash: bug: bare command passed to sash_exec`, 127.
- `int n=$(( (up) ))` before `fn up -> int { return 7 }` printed **0**, status
  0, no diagnostic. `inline_int_func` had `None => return SsaValue::Expr("0")`.
  The sibling comment in `expr_handlers`' nullary-sexpr arm records the *same*
  silent-0 being fixed once before, for a different cause.

**SB5011 cannot catch either, because validate's function table is
whole-program.** Validate says "that's a function, nothing to resolve"; the
transform says "no body yet, must be a command." Each pass is locally
consistent and they mean different things by the word — journal 495's
classifier disagreement one level up, between two *populations* rather than two
predicates.

**No design call to make: DD#81 Part A already has both in its rejected
table**, and states the mechanism ("record each name resolved as an external;
on `fn NAME`, if `NAME` is already in that set, reject"). Three sites resolve a
bareword to an external and **only `cmd_handlers.rs:231` recorded**. The fix is
two copies of five lines that already existed, `lowering_fn_template` guard
included — that guard is what keeps DD#81's *kept* column alive, so
`fn a { echo hi | b }; fn b {…}; a` still compiles (81.43).

**A third hole fell out of the fix.** `echo hi | tr a-z A-Z` then `fn tr {…}`
now rejects — DD#81's *first* rejected row, dynamic shadowing, in the
pipeline-stage position. Accepted the whole time; not found by looking, but by
making the stage path agree with the plain-command path.

Checked every call position forward (plain, `$(f)`, argument, `[[ ]]` operand,
array element, stage first and middle, arith sexpr) — the first five already
rejected, the last two were the holes — and the kept column backward.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-12, latest) — a capture needs a writer, and that is a rule about every `$( )` ══

**The one coverage-queue item parked on DG turned out to be two defects, and
describing it corrected my own filing.** `if x=$(cmd 2>/dev/null)` was told
*"capturing a function's output is not a condition"* with no function in the
program. I had also filed that `if x=$(a | b)` failed the same way — it does
not, and has not since DD#88 shipped. Journal 497.

**DG settled it twice, broadening it the second time.** First: *"so long as the
cmd's stdout remains connected to the caller (e.g., `cmd 2>&1 >f`) it should be
supported."* The example is a counter-example under a strict fd-1 reading, so I
measured rather than asked — a bash differential showed `2>&1 >f` captures
**stderr**, byte-identical in both shells. The rule is not "fd 1 reaches the
caller", it is **"the capture pipe still has a writer"**, which fd 2 satisfies
by copying the pipe before fd 1 leaves. Then: *"the idea that the capture needs
a writer even after redirects makes sense for all captures, not just ones after
`if`"* — which turned a special case into a rule and threw away a
condition-scoped implementation.

**SB4075**, emitted from `validate_expr`'s `CommandSubstitution` arm so it
covers every `$( … )`. `$(cmd >f)` · `>f 2>&1` · `&>f` · `1>&2` · `a | b >f`
are rejected; `2>/dev/null` · `2>&1 >f` · `<in` · `3>&1` · `a >f | b` ·
`$(a >f; b)` are not. **Fully decidable** — SB4048 pins every dup target to a
literal digit run, so there is no conservative arm. Deliberate divergence from
bash, which binds `""` silently.

**Three smaller things the fix needed.** `state.suppressed` is read at emission
time by *one* site, so the new single-command path needed the
`uncheck_block_from` post-pass — extracted as `uncheck_emitted_since` rather
than forked. `$(myfn 2>f)` reaches the relaxed arm where `$(myfn)` never did,
so the function-table check had to move with the relaxation or DD#88's own
target would have slipped through. And `stmt_is_external_command` peeled `-`
and `!` but not `Redirected`, fifteen lines below a caller that already did —
the fifth classifier-wrapper disagreement in as many sessions (journal 495).

**Twelve sweep failures that were not a regression.** `csr.1/2/3/7/8/9`, in
both modes, written *earlier the same session* to pin a silent redirect-drop
bug, every one asserting what SB4075 now rejects. Respelled `2>&1 >f`: same
literal-or-computed target, same `open`, same `dup2`, same `CmdSubstBody` path,
capture still fed — the drop bug stays pinned. **Predicting 8299 first is what
made them unambiguous**; a failing sweep at exactly the predicted total says
the failures are behavioural and the bookkeeping is sound.

Sweep **8299** (8286 passing + 13 skipped), zero failures, twelve flips — all
six ids in both modes, recovering. `mk test` 117. 18 new specs
(`capture_cond.sh` 88.19-88.28, cap4075.1-8).

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-10) — the builtin that was only a name ══

**`kill` was listed as a sash builtin and implemented nowhere.** The string
`"kill"` occurred exactly once in all of `sash/src` — the `BUILTINS` entry in
`validate.rs`, filed under "Process/signal" between `wait` and `signum`. No
`BuiltinCmd::Kill`, no `INTRINSICS` row, no `type_check` entry, no codegen, no
runtime. `kill 0` compiled to a fork/exec of `/usr/bin/kill`, which
`--manifest` confirms.

**Two hand-maintained lists with a stated subset relation and nothing
enforcing it.** The comment above `BUILTINS` claims "a name in BUILTINS is
never PATH-resolved" — and records someone already fixing this exact bug for
`join`, `basename` and `dirname`, whose coreutils twins were being silently
exec'd. But `BUILTINS` membership is *not* what suppresses PATH resolution;
`resolve::is_intrinsic` (`BuiltinCmd` ∪ `INTRINSICS`) is. The claim held for
every other name only because they happen to be in both lists. `kill` was the
one where the coincidence ran out.

**It was also a taint laundering hole.** `is_external_source` reads `BUILTINS`
to decide whether a pipeline stage execs — in a function whose own doc comment
says "a divergence here is a laundering hole". So `kill` exec'd a real external
while being classified non-external, and `kill -l | read x` left `x` clean. It
now raises SB5020.

**DG: "a; prefer parsimony — `kill` is a low volume operation."** Removed from
`BUILTINS`; it is an ordinary external now. On a host that has it, nothing
changes. On a host that does not, the same SB5011 text comes from `validate`
rather than `resolve`.

**The guard is the point.** Removing the entry fixes today; the shape of the
bug invites a recurrence. `every_builtin_name_is_an_intrinsic` and
`value_only_intrinsics_are_all_builtins` now hold the two claims the comments
make. The first was false when written, and was proven capable of failing
before being trusted.

**DG also asked which builtins have external counterparts.** Measured: six —
`kill`, `echo`, `write`, `basename`, `dirname`, `join`. The last three are the
ones the old comment records being fixed. And `mapfile`/`readarray` stay in
`BUILTINS` deliberately: they are `BuiltinCmd`s kept so `retired_bulk_read_diag`
can answer with SB5060 naming the DD#99 replacement, instead of SB5011 sending
the author hunting for a missing binary. Listed to reject *well*.

**How it was found.** The coverage queue flagged nine cold lines in
`resolve_command`, seven of them a duplicate of `validate`'s SB5011. Asking
what could reach them is what surfaced the list disagreement. After the fix
they are unreachable by construction, and stay a diagnostic rather than an
`unreachable!()` — deliberately against the usual rule, because this arm is the
graceful backstop for precisely the drift that `kill` was.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-10) — the exemption that assumed a shell ══

**Three changes, one shape: the compiler held an opinion it had no business
holding, and each time the opinion came from assuming `sash` is a shell.**

**The glob exemption is gone.** `head_is_unjudgeable` (written last session,
by me) exempted a head containing `*`, `?`, `[` or `$` from SB5095 because
"a glob is expanded at runtime". DD#39 is **star-only** — `?` and `[` are not
metacharacters in sash at all — and DG settled the last: **the star glob is
only used with an array**, so in command position `*` is an ordinary filename
byte too. `$` can never reach an `ExprKind::Literal` head (SB5011 rejects it
first). Four characters, four wrong reasons; the exemption re-opened exactly
the compile-time/runtime asymmetry SB5095 exists to close.

`validate.rs`'s `is_valid_command` had the same hole independently and worse:
a bare `ech*` fell through it into the PATH search, so `resolve_on_path` was
never asked about `ech*` at all. DG: "`ech*` should be an error as no such
should exist (does not run `/usr/bin/echo`)." Both gone — `/bin/ech*` is
SB5095, `ech*` is SB5011.

**I verified a behaviour and attributed a cause it did not support.** I ran
`/bin/ec?o` and `/bin/[e]cho`, watched both fail 127, and recorded "globs do
not expand in head position". They failed because they *are* literal. The
inputs could not distinguish the two hypotheses. Reading the DD cost one
query; DG sent me there rather than answering, which was right.

**A path with a space can now be run (SB5096).** It could not before: a bare
word ends at a space and a double-quoted head is SB5011, so `/opt/my tool`
was unsayable — not rejected with a reason, simply absent from the language.
A single-quoted head now denotes a literal command name. DG scoped it in the
same breath: "No superfluous quotes like `'echo'`", so `'echo'` is SB5096 and
the rule is two-sided. Double quotes are **not** the escape hatch; SB5011
stands, because interpolation means there is no single name to resolve.

The "could this have been written bare?" test reuses the lexer's own
`word_ends_here` byte set rather than forking it — a private fork of a shared
walker has bitten this repo twice. The agreement is a **unit test that drives
the real Scanner**, not a comment. The predicate is deliberately biased
towards "needs quoting": a false accept costs redundant quotes, a false
reject would make a real program unsayable.

Normalization happens in `parse_command`, not `validate`. The rest of the
compiler holds "a command head is `ExprKind::Literal`" as an invariant —
`ssa_taint.rs` and `capture_purity.rs` each carry an `unreachable!` naming
SB5011 — so a `SingleQuoted` head surviving parse would ICE in `transform`.
Checked the other six `Command { … }` sites first: all synthesize a literal
from a known name.

**An unreadable `--sysroot` is now a usage error, before compilation starts.**
`squashfs_listing` answered an unreadable image with an empty map, so every
path lookup said "not there" and **every command head in the program**
reported SB5095 — the one real fault, a bad compiler argument, buried under a
diagnostic per line blaming the user's source. Now `check_flags` reports it
and exits; a successful read primes the cache so `unsquashfs` still runs once.
A nonexistent **directory** sysroot has the identical shape and reports the
same way. `cli.31`/`cli.32` pinned the old behaviour and were rewritten — they
never tested the listing parser either (absent image = empty stdout).

**Gates.** Sweep **8079/8079 predicted**, 8066 passing + 13 skipped, **0
flips**, machinery proven capable (248 first-vs-now differences). `mk test`
green. 9 new specs (`qhead.1`-`qhead.9`), dual-mode = +18.

**The complexity gate caught two functions I did not.** `check_sysroot`
landed at cc 9 / cog 8 and `parse_command` at cog 6, both over the 3×
cognitive bar. Split before commit.

**Filed P4:** `exec /bin/ech*` reports SB5029 "inline `*` glob is not allowed
in command arguments" alongside the correct SB5095, because the target sits
in argv position. Misleading advice, not a wrong answer.

**Process failure worth recording.** Three user turns mid-session produced no

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-09, latest) — the parser that nothing had ever parsed with ══

**The coverage queue found a false reject in code one commit old.** Rebuilt
the stale `coverage.db` (19 files renumbered), ranked by function, and the head
of the list was the SB5095 work itself: six functions, **42 cold lines**, the
whole `unsquashfs -ll` parser and symlink follower. I had verified those cases
by hand and said so in journal 486; nothing mechanical held any of it.

**`cli.31`/`cli.32` were why it looked covered.** They point `--sysroot=` at a
*nonexistent* image, so stdout is empty and `parse_squashfs_line` is never
called once — correct end-to-end assertions, zero parser coverage.

**The bug.** A symlink whose target contains `..` — `/usr/bin/x ->
../lib/tool`, how real images spell most cross-directory links — was rejected
as "no such file" though the host agrees it is runnable. The follower looked
up the literal join, and a squashfs listing holds no `..` in any key.
`normalize_path` resolves it lexically now, clamping at the root.

**I nearly fixed a non-bug first.** My initial fixture's `..` link genuinely
dangled, so the rejection was right. What separated them was checking the
fixture against the host rather than against my expectation of it. `sq.4` is
the valid link, `sq.5` the dangling one — and `sq.5` exists so `sq.4` cannot
be satisfied by a follower that stopped checking.

**15 specs (`sq.1`-`sq.15`), no root needed** — `mksquashfs`'s pseudo-file
syntax supplies the device node, `chmod` the mode cases. Each names the format
fact it holds: `sq.8` the device line whose size column is `1,  5` (two fields
where every other line has one); `sq.10`/`sq.11` the setuid pair, where
uppercase `S` must yield 0644 and lowercase `s` 0755 — the reason `triple_bits`
reads the character instead of testing for `x`, which would false-reject every
setuid binary in a real image.

**8 unit tests for what no spec can reach** — a path with a space (SB5011
rejects such a head long before resolution), the `" -> "` split applying only
to `l` modes, and the short-mode-string guard, which exists because
`triple_bits` indexes bytes 1..10 and would otherwise **panic** on malformed
external output.

**Also keyed `SQUASHFS_CACHE`** by image. It was a trap rather than a live bug
— one compile per process — but the comment claimed "per compile" when the
truth was "per process".

Sweep **8061/8061 predicted**, 30 new ids all `sq.*`, **zero flips**; `mk test`

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-09) — the path that was never looked at ══

**SB5095: an absolute command head must be a runnable file.** DG read the
previous entry's behaviour-change flag and asked whether `/nonexistant` should
be caught at compile time. It should have been; it was not. The compiler had a
three-way asymmetry — bare name → SB5011, relative `./x` → SB5051, **absolute
`/x` → compiles, 127 at runtime** — because `is_resolvable_external` returned
`false` for anything containing `/`, so an absolute head was never looked at.
`--manifest` was emitting a dependency it already knew could not be met.
Journal 486, specs `errors.sh` `cmdpath.1`-`cmdpath.17`.

**The obstacle was inside DD#23.** Its "Or chain alternatives" example
(`/usr/bin/grep … || /bin/grep …`) only parses as advice if an absolute path
may be absent — and a hand-written two-entry fallback *is* the search
ambiguity DD#23 exists to forbid. DG approved the rejection; the example is
**withdrawn in an addendum**, not silently edited.

**It names the fault, not just the miss**: `no such file` / `it is a
directory` / `it is not a regular file` / `mode 0444 grants no execute
permission` / `its symlink chain does not terminate`. `PathMiss::LinkLoop`
exists because a cycle first reported "no such file" — a wrong answer wearing
a true answer's clothes, the same call as `waitstatus` returning `-1`.

**A second, pre-existing bug fell out**: `resolve_command_path` tested
`is_file()`, so a mode-0444 candidate early in `PATH` **won** the search and
the failure arrived at `exec` time with the shadowing path baked in. It now
requires executability and keeps looking (`cmdpath.17`).

**The squashfs branch had to be rewritten, not extended.** `unsquashfs -l`
gives names only; type and mode need `-ll` — but `-l` counted a symlink as
present, so rejecting non-regular entries without following links would have
broken every real image (`/bin -> usr/bin`). It now follows, 8-hop capped.

**The harness traded a capability for the rule.** No spec can name a missing
absolute path any more, so `run_sash_vanish` deletes the target *between
compile and run*, in both backends. The spec is now a program whose dependency
vanished underneath it — the only way that runtime path is still reachable,
and a truer description of when it happens in the field.

Scope boundaries are specified, because the one failure SB5095 cannot afford
is a false reject: `[[ -x /path ]]` untouched (DD#23 names it as *the* runtime
existence test), globs untouched (`head_is_unjudgeable` exempts `*?[$`).

Sweep **8031/8031 predicted**, 34 new ids all `cmdpath`, **zero flips**;
`mk test` green. Filed `notes/tasks/target-user-access-check.md` for DG's
`--target-user` parenthetical.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-09) — the latch that answered anyway ══

**DD#126 §2: `wait` no longer touches `$?`.** The reaped child's status goes
to a runtime-owned latch read by a new nullary int intrinsic,
`$(waitstatus)`; on ECHILD it is `-1`. This closes yesterday's "known gap"
below, which was not cosmetic — `while (( wait > 0 )) { int s=$(waitstatus) }`
is the drain loop DD#126 exists for, and the body could not read the status it
had just reaped. Journal 485, specs `commands.sh` `126.21`-`126.36`.

**It subtracts rather than adds.** With the status out of `$?`, the SB5012
exception `stmt_reaps_child` that §1 introduced is **deleted** — `-` means "I
am not handling this" again, with no carve-out. That is why the out-param
alternative lost: `(wait p s)` would have made the sexpr's second operand a
*name*, reintroducing the two-operand-semantics split DD#126 had just removed.

**SB5094 — a latch is readable for exactly one statement.** `$(waitstatus)`
and `$(getcpid)`/`$!` are single-slot and silently overwritten, so a late read
is a plausible wrong number, not an error. This retires
`bug-bg-pid-slot-unavailable` (P1): the `-1` sentinel it offered would have
fixed only the *first* read. The drain loop needs no special case — a `while`
body is already seeded with the state the condition left, and the condition is
the producing statement.

**Two bugs found implementing it.** SB5012 was **blind to the `(( … ))`
statement form** — `direct_exprs` yields nothing for `StmtKind::ArithTest` by
design, so `if (( (status) == 0 ))` read an unavailable status and raised
nothing, while the `$(( … ))` expression form was caught. And `- cmd &` is
`Suppressed(List(Background, …))`, so a latch transition written into the list
arm of the walker fired for `cmd &` and not for `- cmd &`; the producer is now
structural, one authority for every statement shape.

**Visible change:** `/nonexistent &` + `- wait` now exits **0**, not 127. The
127 was a side effect of the deleted exception (an available-but-unconsumed
status at program end *is* the exit status). `int s=$(waitstatus); exit $s` is
the spelling that propagates it — `errors.sh` 55.16, `commands.sh` 126.36.

**Canonical spellings** are `status` / `getcpid` / `waitstatus`, with `$?` and
`$!` as punctuation sugar (DG).

Sweep **7997** (predicted exactly), 0 failing, 0 flips, 32 new ids. `mk test`
green.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-09) — the builtin that aborted because it had nothing to say ══

**DD#126: `wait` is `wait(2)`/`waitpid(2)`, returns the reaped pid or `-1`,
and never aborts.** It was a statement builtin that aborted on `ECHILD`, which
made DG's `while (( wait > 0 )) { : }` drain loop unwritable — the loop's exit
condition was the program's exit. DG declined to invent bash's wait-for-all:
"waiting for all would require a loop". Journal 484, specs `commands.sh`
`126.1`-`126.20`.

**The backend divergence was closed by removing both branches, not by making
them agree.** `bug-wait-backends-diverge-no-children` (native left `$?` at
127, `--emit-c` set 0): `sash_wait_any(pid, status_out)` writes the slot
**only on a successful reap**, and both backends seed it with the current `$?`
and write it back unconditionally. "A reap that found nothing says nothing
about any child" is now an ABI property, and neither backend has a line that
could disagree. Same move as 483's parser desugar.

**`wait` is the first command where `-` and `$?` talk about different
things** — `-` discards the *pid*, and `$(status)` is the only route to the
child's exit — so SB5012 carries one exception, `stmt_reaps_child`. A bare
`wait` is **SB4016** (the unconsumed-value rule, applied; DG's "`-` wait for
I-don't-care" only has content if the bare form is not also it).

**`value_intrinsic_arity` now returns a range**, and all three positions read
it — including the statement spelling `- wait 1 2`, which neither value check
could see and which discarded the surplus in silence. Generalising
`arith_intrinsic_complaint` off that table **newly catches `(getpid x)`**,
previously a silent 0.

**Known gap, reported not closed:** an arithmetic *condition* sets `$?` from
its own verdict, so `while (( wait > 0 )) { … }` cannot read the reaped
child's status in the body. Usable shapes: `int p=$(wait); int s=$(status)`,
or `- wait` + `$(status)`. Matches wait(2)'s out-param; a `waitstatus`
intrinsic would close it and is purely additive.

Sweep **7965** (predicted exactly), 0 failing, 0 flips, 40 new ids. `mk test`
green.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-09) — the rule that promised, and the remedy it removed ══

**DD#125 had been paid for and never collected.** The DD justifies reservation
as the thing that "makes a bare word in arithmetic unambiguous, which is what
lets `$(( wait ))` / `$(( getpid ))` name the intrinsic". Measured at
`4ac831f`, all ten of `getpid getppid argc random signum epochseconds status
getcpid len strlen` still reported SB5031. Meanwhile `$(( f ))` had called a
nullary `-> int` *user* function for as long as int functions existed — the
asymmetry was the whole gap. Journal 483, specs `58.54`-`58.67`.

**The desugar is in the parser, deliberately.** A bare compiler-owned word
becomes the very `FuncCall { args: [] }` node the DD#58 sexpr builds, so
validate / `type_check` / the transform see one shape and cannot drift: bare
`echo` is the same SB4030 as `(echo)`, bare `len` the same SB4045. Three
consumers each recognising a compiler-owned `ArithExpr::Var` would have been
three lists for one question — the shape that rotted one commit earlier.
The lookahead keeps an assignment target a target, so `(( getpid = 5 ))`
still reaches SB5092.

**SB5093 — the rule had removed its own remedy.** `echo $getpid` said
"assign it first"; `int getpid=1` said SB5092. A rule satisfiable only by
breaking another rule. DD#125 created that the day it landed and nothing
noticed, because every spec about it was about *binding*. SB5093 answers the
read side with advice keyed on `ArithDenotation`, ahead of the `${x:-…}`
opt-out — `${getpid:-5}` was never an intentional default, it was a read
of an unbindable name quietly producing `5`. Specs `125.16`-`125.22`.

**The binding half of SB5092 is now the compiler's first gate.** With the
desugar, `int status=5; echo $(( status ))` reported SB5012 from an earlier
batch and masked SB5092 entirely. `check_reserved_names` now takes a
`ReservedScope`: `Bindings` (well-formed nodes) runs first and alone, because
once a program binds `status` no other diagnostic about `status` is
trustworthy; `CommandTargets` stays late, where DD#125 put it so SB5057 wins
for `read -a arr -d :`.

**Two bugs found, recorded, not fixed — both are DG's call.** `$!` /
`$(getcpid)` before any `&` yields a silent empty where `$(status)` has
SB5012; and bare `wait` with no children sets `$?` to 127 natively and 0 under
`--emit-c`, a differential-oracle divergence no spec catches. The second is
DD#126's to fix.

Sweep **7925**, 0 failing, 0 flips, 42 new ids (predicted), self-test 248.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-09, latest) — the list that could not grow ══

**Nineteen names were silently `0` in arithmetic.** `$(( (echo) ))` compiled
and printed `0`; so did `(cd)`, `(read)`, `(break)`, `(argv)`, `(unset)` and
thirteen more. Journal 482, specs `58.36`-`58.53`.

**The cause was a deny-list over an open set.** `is_sexpr_string_producer`
listed twelve string intrinsics and admitted every *other* compiler-owned name
as a valid int producer, which then lowered as a read of an unset variable.
Five of the nineteen are `BuiltinCmd` variants added after that list was
written — they joined the legal class on the day they were declared, with no
edit to the file that decides it.

**One table now, keyed on the enum.** `resolve::ArithDenotation` says `Int` /
`Str` / `Statement` for every compiler-owned name and is **total over
`BuiltinCmd`**, so a new builtin does not compile until it is classified. Two
other lists are deleted: `type_check::is_int_returning_intrinsic` and
`is_sexpr_string_producer` both read the one table, and `resolve::INTRINSICS`
lost the five entries (`argv`, `len`, `strlen`, `keys`, `join`) that
contradicted its own doc by also being `BuiltinCmd` names.

**A statement gets its own message.** "capture it first with `$()`" is good
advice for `toupper` and wrong for `break`, so `Statement` says "`echo` is a
command, not a value — it denotes nothing in arithmetic."

**The first sweep, before any new spec, reported zero flips.** That is the
measurement of the gap: nothing in the suite touched any of the nineteen in
either direction, which is how `bug-arith-sexpr-intrinsics-zero` could be
marked done with two thirds of its own category B still open.

**Gates.** Sweep **7883** (predicted before running), 0 failing, 0 flips, 36
new ids, self-test 248. Units 86/27/20.

**Next:** DD#126 — `wait` as a non-aborting int builtin (wait(2)/waitpid(2),

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-09) — the namespace that was never partitioned ══

**DD#125 landed: a name the compiler already understands is not the user's to
bind.** Keywords + `BuiltinCmd` names + `INTRINSICS`, rejected as a variable,
collection, `for` variable, read target or `fn` name with **SB5092**. Journal
481. DG's rule; it also unblocks bare-word nullary intrinsics in arithmetic
(`$(( wait ))`), which is the next piece.

**What it fixes.** `fn getpid -> int { return 42 }` gave *3444042* in
`$(( (getpid) ))` and *42* in `$(getpid)` — one program, one name, two answers,
because the three resolution positions had three different precedence orders
and none of them was written down. Reservation deletes the question.

**I predicted one broken spec and broke six.** I had grepped for declarations
of reserved names, which is the rule's subject, and missed every program that
binds one through another shape. What worked instead: instrument `chk` to log
any spec emitting SB5092, run every file, read the list.

**Three defects DG caught in my framing, all real.** `read` has no flags
(DD#99) yet the read-target extractor still filtered `-`-prefixed args — which
made SB5092 fire on a delimiter and *mask* SB5057. `SubshellStart` emits
`sash_fork()` for `cmd &`, so it was named after the construct DD#38 removed →
`ForkBackground`. `__` is not a sigil (DD#100's sigil is `=`) → `sigil_str` is
now `internal_name`. I had propagated all three misnomers into a journal, four
specs and a commit message without checking them against the DDs.

**The nine `__` names were a leak, not a namespace.** DG asked *why* they
exist: `SsaInst::Command` carries a redundant `name: String` beside its `kind`,
so a synthesised command invents a name by spelling the enum out. `from_name`
then had to map them back — one classifier answering for both compiler-invented
and user-typed names. Nothing reads that direction (every backend dispatches on
`kind`; the string is write-only, which is why all nine arms were cold). So the
arms were **deleted from `from_name`** rather than reserved. A `__` name typed
by a user is now an ordinary SB5011. `cov.327`-`cov.330` pass unchanged.

**A spec that had stopped testing its subject.** `25.6` names the runtime
SUB-overflow trap but defined `fn sub` and called it — `sub` is a value
intrinsic, so the call was SB5073 at *compile* time and the assertion
(`rc != 0 && -z $out`) was satisfied by the compile error. Predates DD#125.
Renamed `subtract`, assertion tightened with `-z $err`, trap now fires. The
general shape: **`rc != 0` with no claim about which error will accept any
future error.**

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-08) — the producer I did not check ══

**Coverage queue, four more candidates.** One spec gap on an everyday idiom,
one dead branch deleted, one duplicate destructuring merged, ten mirrored ICE
arms collapsed to one shared site. Journal 479.

**`emit_degenerate_pipeline` deleted.** Its 0-/1-stage guard was unreachable:
`lower_pipeline_body` only builds an `SsaInst::Pipeline` for
`commands.len() > 1` and every pusher contributes one stage per command. The
native backend had no such guard and would have wrapped `n - 1` on a `usize`.
A defensive branch in `emit_c` — the *differential oracle* — that silently
normalises what native mishandles is the oracle absorbing the difference it
exists to report. Both now call `ssa::pipeline_num_pipes`, which ICEs instead.

**And I got that ICE's floor wrong, which is the finding worth keeping.** I
wrote `n > 1` for both forms; `spec/taint.sh` failed fifteen checks. A capture
pipeline (`cmd | readline x`) carries only the **producers**,
`commands[..len-1]` — two commands, one stage. I had traced one of the three
producers of `SsaInst::Pipeline` and generalised. Journal 439 said this in the

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-08) — the rule that stopped at the declaration ══

**Sixteen broken spellings of plain assignment. Seven segfaulted.** Found by
writing a spec for a cold line in `handle_append_assign` — the map-append path,
cold because no spec appends to a map. The first spelling tried ICEd the
compiler.

```
array a=(x y)
a=z              # SIGSEGV. `len a` reports 0.
a=$(echo hi)     # SIGSEGV
map m=([a]=1)
m=(y)            # silently emptied the map
m+=([b]=2)       # compiler ICE
```

Nothing checked that an assignment's value matched the variable's kind. `a.op`
is read at three sites in `validate.rs`, all taint, all acting on `Set`.

**DD#117 fixed this a fortnight ago — for declarations.** It said, in the
sentence that granted it: *"Append remains available as a statement, once the
name is declared."* That is true, and it handed the same segfault to the next
line. It also folded `Array` and `AssocArray` into one `Collection`, so
`array a=([b]=2)` passed its own rule and silently emptied `a`.

**DD#124.** An assignment's value must have the shape of the target's kind
(SB5090) — three kinds, not two. DG's call on the one case DD#117's principle
did not settle: *"reject += on maps - favor clarity over compatibility with
bash"* (SB5091). bash merges; a map has no end to append to, and `m[key]=value`
already works.

One classifier shared by SB4064 and SB5090, total over `(TargetKind,
InitShape)` with the no-wildcard marker — keeping two copies is how DD#117's
blind spot would have been reproduced in the new code. SB5055 keeps the scalar
target (it names the missing declaration); it was missing the `([k]=v)` shape.
`handle_append_assign` lost its map branch: the cold lines that started this.

(nothing happened in between). Parameter is `SsaValue`/`SsaInst`/a rendered

handling a rejected spelling reads as *support* for it. Measured before

the arm becomes **reachable**. Where the gate rejects every spelling, delete,

**A bug, found by a cold line.** `${ … }` as a subscript index worked in three
spellings and was SB4035 in two:

```
$(( a[${i}] ))      0        $(( ${a[${i}]} ))   SB4035
```

`scan_arith_braced_var` ended a braced body at the **first** `}`, so

scanner. It was a *second* subscript scanner, grown beside the one whose doc
comment says "do not grow a second scanner for either caller" — the comment
did not stop it because it addressed `[ … ]` callers and this one scans
`{ … }`. The shared scan was already generic over `[] {} ()`; only its entry
was pinned to `[`. Generalised to `balanced_close`, with
`balanced_subscript_close` as a `[`-only wrapper. Specs `80.123`-`80.130` pin
all four spellings, one of them reading the same cell four ways in one
program.

rendered text, not just the code — a multiplier stuck at 1 still accepts `4K`,

overflows *only after* scaling.

**A cold line can be a measurement fault.** `lib.rs:216` was in the queue, and
`cli.6` provably executes it. Exporting that run's own profraw reads 1;
merging the sweep's 45 reads 0, having passed through `18446744073709551614`
(= −2) on the way. LLVM derives a loop body's count from the back-edge, and a
`std::process::exit` from inside the loop increments one side and never the
other; the error accumulates across profraws until it swamps the true count.
Checked across the whole 470-line cohort, **exactly one line was wrong** — so
it is rare, but silent. The detection (export one profraw; a single process
cannot underflow) is now in AGENTS.md.

all-separators arm said `for (( ;; ))` reaches it, and spec `31.51` asserted
the same reading for its whole life. It does not: the header splits into three

caught it. `$(( ; ))` is the real spelling. A spec pins behaviour; it does not

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-04) — a cell is a variable ══

`mk test` rc=0, fmt/clippy clean. Sweep **7565 → 7609**, the predicted +44
(22 specs, dual-mode), zero failures. Journal 469. **DD#123 added.**

**The rule.** DG authorised two surface changes and supplied the rule they
share — *"a string cell behaves like a string variable"* — applied this time
to all its consequences rather than the case in front of me. A cell reads
where a variable reads, takes the dispositions a variable takes, owes the
same string→int crossing.

**1. `$(( $a[1] ))` reads the cell.** The SB4035 reject was right when it was
written: in August `$a` and `[i]` were separate tokens and the arith body's
reconstruct/re-lex round trip re-spaced the index, silently reading `a[0]`.
The task file said a correct fix had to fuse `$name[…]` into one token at the
lexer — which is exactly what `braceless_subscript` has done since 2026-10-03,
built for DD#80's "all paths must agree". **The carve-out was guarding against
a defect the same function had already fixed**, and I was the one who carried
it forward. Removing `if self.arith_depth > 0` was the whole change. The
spelling now agrees with `${a[i]}` on the rejects too (`$a[i+1]` SB4041, not an
lvalue).

**2. `$a[0]:-z` is a disposition** — DD#90's scope list gains a fourth entry.
A *correctness* fix, not ergonomics: brace-less, `$a[9]:?missing` printed
`:?missing` and exited **0** — a guard that could not fail — and `:~` passed an
argument where the braced form passes none (a DD#84 arity difference). DG
floated a legibility limit ("bordered by a space"); measured, **that limit
already ships** — the `:` must be tight or it isn't a disposition, for scalars
since DD#90. No cell-specific rule, which would have been a third grammar.
The arith ternary collision is a loud SB4020, as it already is for `$x:-5`.

**3. The bug: `$(( ${s[0]} ))` on a string array silently read 0.** Bare
`s[0]` has been SB4030 since 2026-08-19; the braced spelling never was, because
`walk_arith_subscripts` ended in `_ => {}` and swallowed `ArithExpr::Expansion`.
Six weeks, and since model B makes bare `m[k]` inexpressible, **no map cell had
ever been checked at all**. **The fourth non-total IR walker to be the bug.**
Now total, with the `do not add a wildcard` marker.

The first fix flagged `(strlen ${a[1]})` — a *string* argument to an intrinsic,
not an int operand. Rather than fork `walk_arith_var_reads` (a hazard this repo
has a memory for), one private total `walk_arith_int_operands` with two views:
the `FuncCall`-skip decision now lives in one place. Six specs (asx.1–asx.6)
pinned the old reading and were re-pointed, each keeping its subject.

**Also:** the SB4035 hint was *not* dead — stray brackets still reach it — but
its text had become false; reworded. `bare_map_subscript_error` is type-aware,
so a string map's author isn't sent to `${m[k]}`, which also rejects.

**`:-` targets the additive identity** (`""` / `0`) — sash has no unset. That

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-04) — the pipe binds to the reader ══

`mk test` rc=0. Sweep **7543 → 7565**, the predicted +22 (11 specs,
dual-mode), zero failures. Journal 468. **DD#122 added.**

**The rule, now written down.** DG: *"`readline` or `while readline` without
a leading pipe would read fd 0; `cmd | while readline v` would read the
output of `cmd`; a `/bin/cat` within that `cmd | while` would read fd 0."*
A pipe binds to the **reader**, never to fd 0 — which follows from the loop
running in the **parent**, the thing that makes `cmd | while readline v; do
(( n = n + 1 )); done` leave `n` set where bash prints `0`. It had never been
recorded; I inferred the opposite from the code twice.

**The bug.** `repoint_readlines_to_pipe` walked every block lowered so far,
so a `readline` with **no pipe at all** was captured by a later pipeline and
aimed at its exhausted pipe — `MID=[]`, exit 0, no diagnostic, both backends.
Delete the unrelated pipeline above it and the identical statement is
correct. Now scoped to the instructions the final stage's own lowering
produced (`mark_ssa` / `for_each_new_inst`). **The array half
(`rewrite_lastpipe_consumer_fds`) had the identical defect** — and my first
spec for it asserted nothing, passing against the unfixed compiler, which the
verify-it-fails-first check caught.

**One sentinel, one spelling.** Native initialised `pipe_read_fd_var` to `0`
(a *valid* fd, so a stray sentinel silently read stdin and looked correct);
`--emit-c` wrote `-1` and aborted rc=99 in rustix. Both `-1` now.

**Two new rejections, DD#122 §3.** SB4022 extended to the final stage —
`cmd | { … }` / `| if` / `| for` fork and discard everything they assign,
which is what DD#38 rejects `( … )` for, through a different syntactic door;
the advice stays "wrap it in a function", verified byte-identical to bash.
SB4073 is new: a `while` final stage with no `readline`/`read` in it had the
producer's output go nowhere. `is_while_read` stays structural and is now
*correct*, because SB4073 guarantees what it assumed — a rival became a
backstop.

**DD#116 closed out.** Three rivals deleted (`detect_array_iter`'s
`DoubleQuoted` and `Redirected` arms, which stated the opposite of SB5026 /

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-04) — the index that was never an index ══

Sweep **7517** (3861 native, 3643 c + 13 skipped), zero failures, predicted
exactly. `mk test` rc=0. Journals 464 and 465. Two bugs, found from the
coverage queue, plus the queue itself.

**A silent miscompile.** `m[$s ] x ]="z"` compiled clean and **discarded
source** — it assigned the literal `]=9` to key `zz`, dropping ` x ` without a
diagnostic. Two coupled parser defects: the shape probe searched for a `]`
*followed by* `=`/`+=` while the consumer took the *first* `]` (two searches,
two predicates, one bracket), and `parse_assignment` then did
`scanner.next(); // consume =` **unconditionally** — consuming whatever stood
there as if it were the operator. Harmless on an int array, where a second `]`
is not expressible; reachable on a map, where a string key makes it legal.
Now one search (`lhs_index_close_from`) and an explicit `match` on the
operator.

**DD#80 was not enforced on the write side at all.** Every ambiguous index
form that rejects when *read* was accepted when *written*: `m[ a b ]=`,
`m[a-b]=`, `m[a.b]=`, `m[ ] ]=`, and `m[ $s x ]=` — which stored the
**unexpanded** text `$s x` as the key. The cause is a shape: an assignment's
LHS index is a bare `Expr` in `Assignment.index`, never wrapped in an
`ExprKind::Subscript`, so `flag_subscript_index` *reached* it and could not
tell it was an index. Fixed with a second visitor, `flag_assignment_index`,
calling the same `ambiguous_index_diag`. One rule, two IR shapes.

**Third time.** DD#80 enforcement has now proved position-dependent rather
than rule-dependent three times — the write surface (2026-09-26), the
assignment/declaration value (journal 462), and this. The question to ask is
not "does the check fire on `${a[K]}`" but "what are all the IR shapes an
index can inhabit".

Five forms flipped to SB4041; the nine legal write spellings were measured
before and after and are untouched. SB4041 lost the word "braced" — it is one
rule for all positions now. Specs: `subscript.sh` sections P and Q,
`80.97`-`80.113` (+17 ids).

**Coverage, resumed — the ranking was mostly ICEs.** Union at `aab5868`:
**97.55% lines, 98.78% functions, 98.12% regions, 91.27% branches**, 518
uncovered lines. The long-standing head of the by-function ranking,
`emit_c.rs::lower_value_as_str_aggregate` (6 cold), is **six `panic!` ICE
arms** — correctly cold, and they must stay cold. Classifying the whole
cohort by contiguous cold run: **64 runs are ICE arms (1 line each), 368 runs
/ 454 lines are not**. Ranking by raw cold-line count over-weights multi-line
`Err(…)` expressions — the top three non-ICE runs are documented-unreachable
arms from the commit above, 5 lines each only because rustfmt spreads them.

**The one real gap: `if attest k v in m` was specced nowhere.**
`AttestKind::of` has one caller and three arms mapping 1:1 onto `AttestForm`;
the array arm had 7 specs, the map arm **0**. That matters because
`div.15`/`div.16` exist for the array arm specifically to pin
`bug-caught-attest-all-fail-path-undefined-handle`, a **SIGSEGV** from an
attested version defined on one path only — and the map form reaches the same
`AttestKind::Coll` lowering. It works: both merge paths correct, the retag
lands, and 60.30's both-binders rule holds in the `if` position too. Five
specs, `div.33`-`div.37` (taint.sh), both backends. Verified warm afterwards
(count 0 → 12; uncovered 518 → 513). Journal 465.

**Next in the queue**, with the ICE arms excluded:
`transform/statements.rs:449` (`hoist_arith_mutations`, `ArithExpr::Ternary`),
`transform/stmt_handlers.rs:912`/`944` (compound and function pipeline

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-03, latest) — all paths must agree ══

Sweep **7473** (3839 native, 3621 c + 13 skipped), zero failures, predicted
exactly. `mk test` rc=0. Journal 463.

DG, on a message of mine written entirely in braced spellings: *"I thought
braceless array access was supported..."* — it is (his decision B, 2026-06-21),
but measuring found the brace-less spelling takes a **different index grammar**
from the braced one, and the interpolated spelling a third, narrower still.
Three parse paths, three answers: `echo $a[$i]` printed an element while
`echo "$a[$i]"` was SB5064, and `$a[$(( i ))]` was SB5064 where the braced
form computed the index.

**DG ruled: "all paths must agree."**

**The fix is a desugar, not a third parser.** The lexer rewrites `$a[K]` and
`"$a[K]"` into `${a[K]}`, so DD#80's grammar is the only subscript grammar in
the compiler and the spellings *cannot* drift again. `try_subscript_arm`,
`try_split_subscript_arm`, `try_emit_array_subscript_in_string` and
`subscript_expr` are deleted. Same mechanism DD#90 uses for `$x:-foo`.

**I filed the wrong recommendation first** (codify the narrowing) and reversed
it on measuring the *scalar* rows: SB5068 exists because `${s[0]}` once
segfaulted, yet `str s=z; echo $s[$(( 0 ))]` compiled and printed `z[0]`. A
safety diagnostic one spelling walks around is not a fix.

**Five ICEs closed by construction.** `$#[0]`, `$?[0]`, `$$[0]`, `$![0]`,
`$1[0]` all panicked with *"ICE: undefined array"*; every braced counterpart
was already clean. SB5031 (`$@[0]`) was a point-fix for two members of this
same family, and its own doc describes the crash.

**Two specs pinned the old asymmetry and were repointed, not deleted** —
`80.34` (now SB4030, with `80.34b` as its braced twin) and `cov.110` (now
SB4041).

Specs: `subscript.sh` sections N and O, `80.70`-`80.96` (+28 ids).

### Two questions for DG

1. **Arithmetic.** `$(( $a[1] ))` is still SB4035 by design (DD#79 model B;
   specs `dsx.1`/`dsx.2`), and the desugar is gated on `arith_depth == 0` to
   keep it that way. But the *stated reason* for that rejection — "can't
   preserve a `$`/variable index cleanly, it would silently read `a[0]`" — is
   dissolved by the desugar. Keep the reject as a choice, or let it through?
2. **Cell dispositions.** `$a[0]:-z` is literal concat; `${a[0]:-z}` is the
   disposition. Filed as `notes/tasks/cell-braceless-disposition.md` — and it
   is not merely ergonomic: `$a[9]:?m` **does not abort**, it yields the string
   `":?m"` with rc 0, so a brace-less guard on a cell is a check that cannot
   fail. `$a[9]:~` likewise emits a literal argument instead of eliding one.
   DD#90's scope list names `$name` / `$N` / `@name` and omits cells, but
   `spec/arithmetic.sh`'s own header for the braced cell dispositions cites
   "a string cell behaves like a string variable" as their basis. (The in-string
   path correctly takes no brace-less disposition — braces required in
   interpolation, already settled.)

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-03) — a capture is not an index ══

Sweep **7417** (3811 native, 3593 c, 13 skipped), zero failures, predicted
exactly. `mk test` rc=0. Journal 462. Commit `5ac1b2b`.

DG ruled on the fork left open at the end of 461: *"I don't think `arr[$(f)]`
is legal, but `arr[$((f))]` where `f` is an int returning fn seems fine."*

**The rule never moved.** DD#80 §2 already says an indexed array's index must
be int-typed, and `is_int_index` is one line — `is_integer_literal(expr) ||
expr_type(expr, env) == VarType::Int`. A capture types as String, so it had
been answering DG's question correctly all along. It was not being asked:
`check_assignment` and `check_declaration` walked their **target's** subscript
and never their **value**. So `echo "${arr[$(f)]}"` was SB4030 while
`str z=${arr[$(f)]}` compiled and printed `q`.

**`functions.sh` lift.3 was pinning the hole** — it asserted the acceptance,
which is why I reverted this fix in 461 rather than deciding for DG. It is now
a rejection, with lift.3b/lift.3c pinning the legal form.

**The ICE was the same missing walk.** `str v="${a[foo]}"` panicked at
`codegen/values.rs:1426` — *"non-integer literal `foo` reached int lowering;
type_check (SB4030) should have rejected it"*, the compiler naming the pass
that never ran. I had filed it as a separate defect. Same four lines close it.

**The capture gets its own diagnostic**, because the generic advice is a dead
end: `${a[$(( $(f) ))]}` is SB4041 and `int i=$(f)` is SB4030. Declaring
`fn f -> int` is the only migration, so the message names it.

DD#80 gained an addendum — notable mainly because this is the **second** time
its enforcement proved position-dependent rather than rule-dependent (the
first was the write surface, 2026-09-26). Both times the rule was fine and a
walk was missing.

Specs: `functions.sh` lift.3/3b/3c, `types.sh` 75.157-75.165.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-03, latest) — why walk that portion again? ══

Sweep **7395** (3800 native, 3582 c, 13 skipped), zero failures, predicted
exactly. `mk test` rc=0. Journal 461. Commit `55e0214`.

DG, on three options I had filed with no recommendation: *"once you find an
error in part of the tree, why walk that portion again? seems like that is a
recipe for numerous errors."* He was not picking from the list — he was asking
why the list existed. Measuring the reframing broke the filing twice.

**It was never about for-in headers.** My comparison table used `keys`
throughout, and `keys` is the one intrinsic validate permits in a for-header
`$( )` and rejects nearly everywhere else — so every "reports once" row was a
program already rejected one pass earlier. The duplication is general to a
command argument: `echo "$(join s X)"` reported **twice**, and with two bad
arguments, **four** times.

**And there were not two walkers.** `check_subscript_in_stmt` was a private
copy of `check_command`'s operand-check tail that also descended into `$( … )`,
while `check_stmt` already walks `cmdsub_bodies()` unconditionally and runs the
full check on each inner statement. My table of "differences" was a table of
drift between two copies of one thing. Third instance of that pattern —
journals 441, 456, now this.

**The drift was load-bearing.** The copies diverged in opposite directions
(`check_len_operand` only in the fork, `check_int_sink_operands` only in the
original), so `len`-on-a-scalar was caught where the fork reached and nowhere
else. `str j="$(len s)"` compiled and `j` was `"2"` — the byte-length overload
`dd75-len-collection-only-strlen` (status **done**) deleted. The duplicate
diagnostic was not the bug; it was the only visible symptom of a redundant walk
whose other half was a silent hole.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-02) — `keys m k`, the DD#75 key snapshot ══

Sweep **7377** (3791 native, 3573 c, 13 skipped), zero failures, predicted
exactly (7345 + 2×16). `mk test` rc=0. Journal 460. Commit `e9b452e`.

DD#75 §3 had promised a map's keys could be *"iterated or snapshotted into an
array"*. Only the first half existed — `$(keys m)` was legal in a `for`-in
header and nowhere else. DG chose the out-param (option (b)): **`keys m k`**,
mirroring DD#60's `argv [N] a`.

**The arity is the whole discriminator.** One argument is the splat, two is the
fill. `argv` carries a `check_argv_form_*` walker family only because `argv a`
and `argv 1` are both arity 1 and something must arbitrate; `keys` has no such
collision, so this is one function (`keys_form_diag`) hung off
`check_command_head`'s existing `CmdPos`. I had planned the `argv` shape before
noticing there was nothing for it to decide.

**The snapshot is clean**, where `argv a` is tainted — the one deliberate
divergence. argv's bytes come from outside the program; a map's keys were put
there by it. Enumerated and ran every route first rather than citing DD#93,
because journal 459 is the record of what citing it was worth.

**Fourteen files, and almost none of it was the feature.** The runtime function
is nine lines. The rest is *registration*: six by-name registries a new fill
must join (`collect_read_targets`, `insert_auto_collection_target`,
`flag_fill_target`, `command_writes_args`, `type_check`'s dispatch, and
removal from `VALUE_ONLY_INTRINSICS`), none exhaustive-checked. `keys` stays
**out** of `bulk_fill_targets` on purpose — that list means "writes from
outside" and feeds SB5067.

**One gap found by probing, not by a test.** `keys m args` compiled and wrote
the immutable function-args array, though `argv args` and `read args` are both
SB5052. Found by deliberately trying reserved names after the feature already
worked.

Two doc comments the change falsified, both corrected: `cmdsub_arity_diag`
claimed `match` was the only name that is both a value intrinsic and a legal
statement, and `sole_cmdsub_command` pointed at a rule that moved in this
commit.

The complexity gate rejected `flag_fill_target` (cog 6 vs a 5.4 ceiling) and
was right to — it had been accumulating by-name arms for four builtins. Split
into `fill_target_spec` and `is_valid_fill_target`.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-02) — the counter-example that was a bug ══

Sweep **7345** (3775 native, 3557 c, 13 skipped), zero failures, predicted

for one found **three defects**, all now fixed.

**1. `map m = @{a:!~}` dropped the DD#91 vouch** (P1). The DD says the bypass
*"is applied in both taint passes so they agree"*. They did not: this compiled
past `validate` and died at the **use** on the SSA backstop — no SB code, no
span, an internal version name. `SsaInst::MapFromArray`'s `mode` collapses

**2. Every bulk fill accepted a map target** (P1). `map m; read m` compiled

and was silently discarding the line into a collection (`len=0`).

exist.** It called a tainted *array* a map, advised an `attest k v in a` that

predates `:!`, so the fourth route was real — but a vouched map is **clean**.
Re-checked all four by hand post-fix: `@{a:~}`/`@{a:-X}` → SB5020,
`m[k]=$tainted` → SB5021, `read m`/`argv m`/`match … m` → SB4030, `@{a:!~}` →
clean by the author's vouch. `keys` is unconditionally clean, as claimed.

## ══ (2026-10-02) — the line stream that was word splitting ══

Sweep **7293** (3749 native, 3531 c, 13 skipped) — predicted two independent
ways before running, zero failures. `mk test` rc=0. Journal 458. DD#28
addendum.

Coverage mining turned up a P1 cluster. `try_dispatch_cmdsubst` rewrote
`for x in $( … )` into `cmd | while readline x`, building **one pipeline stage
per statement** in the capture body. Three silent miscompiles:

- `$(echo a; echo b)` → `echo a | echo b`, so only `b` survived (bash: both)
- `$(echo a | cat)` → a `Pipeline` stmt is not a `Command`, the stage was
  silently dropped, loop ran **zero** times (bash: `a`)
- `$(g)` on a user fn → no DD#23 resolution, bare name to `sash_exec`, the
  compiled program aborted rc=127

The first and third reproduce in plain, fully-taint-checked code. The same
captures in assignment and argument position were correct throughout.

**DG rejected all three of my fix options.** I had assumed `for x in $(cmd)`
should iterate something; he pointed out that capturing the whole `$( )` as if
assigned to a variable is the least surprising reading, that sash has no word
splitting (`read -a` and `match` are the splitting mechanisms), and that this
is therefore a for-loop over a single value — which SB5009 already rejects.

The spec file had said so all along: `cov.61` pinned `$(echo a b c)` producing
one iteration and called the divergence from bash deliberate. The construct was
never a loop; splitting the capture on newlines was word splitting on a
different delimiter.

So: `is_scalar_value_intrinsic` → **`is_collection_intrinsic`** (`argv`, `keys`),
stated in the positive so the rule denies by default — the old polarity is what
let every command, pipeline, sequence and user function fall through. `$(< file)`
rejected alongside: same exemption, same wording, same one-iteration behaviour.
104 lines of lowering deleted. SB5009's message now names the replacements.

`$(argv; CMD)` still reports **SB5025**, the more specific complaint DG settled
2026-09-29 — the new rule defers when the body holds a collection intrinsic.
DG: *"there is no sane way to combine argv or keys with subsequent commands"* —
right, and checking it showed my first cut deferred only to SB5025 on the false
belief that `keys` had none. It has **SB5073**, almost the same sentence, so
`$(keys m; …)` was getting a noisy SB5009+SB5073 double. Deferral made
symmetric; `fs.14` pins that SB5009 does not fire.

Specs: `fs.8` flipped to a rejection, `fs.10`–`fs.13` added for the four shapes,
`cov.61` retired with the code it covered (and with the c-backend EOF
divergence it carried). Also landed: `sw.20`–`sw.25` from the previous session's
`--no-taint` attest arms, and two stale `read -r` comments fixed in
`stmt_handlers.rs` / `pipelines.rs`.

## ══ STATUS (2026-10-02) — the polarity that never had to exist ══

Sweep **7275** (3740 native, 3522 c, 13 skipped) — predicted exactly, zero
failures. `mk test` rc=0. Journal 457 addendum 3. DD#121 addendum.

**DG: "the `if ! attest` can be understood as `if attest { } else {...}`; if
the unmodified form is too vexing, why not translate?"** I had filed that
defect with two options — support the negated form and pay for a polarity flag
in both R2's resolution check and the SSA merge, or reject it with an honest
diagnostic. The translation is a third option that makes the expensive one
cheap:

```
if ! attest C { A } else { B }   ==>   if attest C { B } else { A }
```

No negated caught attest reaches the analysis at all, so the two places that
would have carried a polarity never learn the form exists. Their "resolve" and
"divert" arms cannot drift out of step, which is the failure mode that made
option (a) expensive — and which has produced three separate bugs this week.

**`if ! attest` now behaves identically to the canonical spelling** on both
backends, pass path and divert path, matching bash.

**The filing's stated cause was wrong.** It named
`StmtKind::Negated(Box<Statement>)`; that variant only ever appears as a stage
inside a multi-stage pipeline. A standalone `! cmd` is
`StmtKind::Pipeline { negated: true }`. I had matched on the variant's name
without checking what constructs it. Corrected in the task file.

**Where it lives was the real decision.** A post-parse pass would need a
mutable cmdsub walker, which does not exist — `structural_bodies_mut`
deliberately excludes `$( … )` bodies and says a rewriting pass "has to say
so". Writing one means mirroring `walk_own_exprs` over ~31 `ExprKind`
variants: a second implementation of a shared walker. Instead the rewrite sits
in `parse/parser.rs::make_if`, the constructor **both** spellings of `if` now
build through, so the form is unrepresentable rather than unhandled and every
`if` anywhere is covered — including inside a `$( … )` — with no walker at
all. Precedent was next door: `parse_if_brace` already desugars `else if`.

Two things a naive translation gets wrong, both pinned:

- **`elif` nests rather than swaps** — the chain hangs off the *unnegated*
  condition being false, so `if !C {A} elif C2 {B} else {D}` is
  `if C { if C2 {B} else {D} } else {A}`. A swap here would be a miscompile.
  Verified against bash on all three outcomes (`div.30`, `div.31`).
- **Scope is attest-only** — `if ! /bin/true` works today and `--emit-ir`
  faithfully reports `:negated true`. A blanket rewrite would change a
  documented DD#104 seam for programs unrelated to attest (`div.32`).

**DD#121 is not amended in substance.** No new form reaches the analysis, only
a spelling that is normalised away before validate runs; the three caught
forms are still the three it knows. A pointer was added so a reader knows the
spelling is accepted.

**Left alone deliberately:** bare `! attest …` and `while ! attest …` still
report SB5088. I checked whether that was a ragged edge from my fix — it is
not. **`while attest` is rejected unnegated too, with the same message**, so
the objection is not about `!` but about the position not being a caught form,
and the wording is equally wrong in the unnegated spelling. Filed as
`sb5088-wording-for-non-caught-attest-positions` (P3) rather than smuggled in
because it was nearby.

Complexity gate rejected `flip_negated_attest` at cc 6 / cog 9; extracted two
helpers rather than bypassing. All five new functions cc ≤ 2, cog ≤ 1.

Specs `div.24`-`div.32` in `spec/taint.sh` (`plan=326`).
