`transform/control_flow.rs::lower_if_attest` now merges via the shared
`insert_phis_two_branch`. It was the **only** one of the transform's six
two-branch merges that did not.

**Reading it against R2 found a bigger fault than the one filed.** Its
comment claimed to restore the pre-attest version at the merge, justified as
deliberate because SB5089 left "no clean version to merge to" — R2 is the
guarantee that there *is* one. And the restore ran only in the **no-else**
case: with an `else`, the state leaked out of the else branch, so
`if attest x …; then echo t; else x=d; fi; echo $x` lowered to a merge
reading **the else-branch version, defined on exactly one path**. That is the
journal 449/450 hazard, in the code citing journal 449 as the reason not to
touch it. Latent only because codegen collapses a scalar's versions to one
slot.

Now: resolve → `PHI x_4 <- [(then, x_2), (else, x_3)]`; divert → `x_2`, the
attested version, no phi (the diverting else is not a predecessor, so the
then-state *is* the merge state — which keeps the attested version off every
path where it is undefined). `block_falls_through` is `pub(crate)` and shared
with the transform, not duplicated: the predicate deciding "is this else a
predecessor" must be the one `validate` uses for "is this path exempt".

the collection attest-all failure that was once
`bug-caught-attest-all-fail-path-undefined-handle`. div.10-div.16.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-30) — the second desugar path; SB5012 reaches into arithmetic ══

Sweep **7163** (3684 native, 3466 c, 13 skipped) — predicted exactly, twice,
zero failures, no retirements. `mk test` rc=0. Journal 455.

**DG corrected the direction of the desugar.** I had found the transform
rewriting `getpid`/`status`/`getcpid` into `$`/`?`/`!`, noticed the codegen
arms for those intrinsics were cold, and concluded the arms were dead by
construction. Backwards: DD#111 says *"the intrinsic is the real thing"*, so
the rewrite is the violation and the arms are what it starves.

Splitting the three by whether anything *writes* the slot separated them
cleanly. `status`→`?` has four `define` sites and `getcpid`→`!` has one —
those are **stateful**, and reading the slot *is* the lowering. `getpid`→`$`
had **zero**: a pure rename, and exactly the one whose arms were cold. It is
gone, along with the four `"$"` special-cases in `codegen/values.rs`,
`emit_c.rs` and `ssa_taint.rs`. `magic_intrinsic_var` is now
`stateful_intrinsic_slot` and holds only what the name claims.

**"Provably dead by grep" is not proof — twice, on the same code.** I deleted
those special-cases on the strength of a grep for `define("$")`, rebuilt, and
`echo $(( $$ > 0 ))` printed 0. There was a **second, independent desugar
path**: `parse/arith.rs::scan_arith_dollar` has its own single-character scan
for `$#`/`$?`/`$$`/`$!` and never consulted the word path's table. The grep
could not have found it — the arith lexer assembles the name a character at a
time. Both paths now share `magic_sugar_intrinsic`.

**The invariant guard was blind by type.** `assert_no_magic_sugar` exists to
make a missed construction site loud instead of silent, and its doc *predicts*
that a miss would leave "SB5012's `$?` state machine" not seeing reads. It
walks `ExprKind`; `ArithExpr::DollarVar` is a different type. The prediction
was not hypothetical — it had already come true.

**So: SB5012 was blind to arithmetic status reads** (P2, pre-existing at HEAD,
confirmed by `git stash`). With no preceding command, `echo "$?"` and
`echo "$(status)"` were correctly rejected while `echo $(( $? ))`,
`echo $(( (status) ))` and `int n=$(( (status) ))` were **accepted**, yielding
0. Same root cause one layer down: `find_status_reads` walks `Expr` nodes and
an arithmetic `(status)` is an `ArithExpr::FuncCall`.

**And the walker it wanted to reuse had a wildcard.**
`walk_arith_intrinsic_calls` spelled out its own recursion behind `_ => {}`,
swallowing `Subscript` and `SubscriptAssign` — both carry `ArithExpr` children,
so `$(( a[(status)] ))` stayed blind even after the `Expr` half was fixed. Its
one other caller is the sexpr **arity** check, blind under a subscript index
for exactly as long. Descent now delegates to the already-total
`ArithExpr::children()`. Fourth non-total IR walk to be the bug in recent
sessions; this one was hiding two variants that had been there all along.

`spec/arithmetic.sh` `as.1`-`as.8` (`plan=338`→`346`). None of the five
pre-existing specs that read status inside arithmetic needed touching — every
one has a preceding command, which is the point of the rule.

Three functions tripped the complexity gate on the way in; extracting

them under. The gate was right — each had grown a second job.

**Housekeeping:** `notes/status.md` carried **five** "latest" markers, stale
back to 2026-09-29. Demoted to this one.

**Back to coverage.** Fresh `mk cov-union` + `mk cov-db`. `getpid` is now

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-30) — a for-in source must denote a collection ══

Sweep **7147** (3676 native, 3458 c, 13 skipped) — predicted exactly, zero
failures, no retirements. `mk test` rc=0. Journal 454.

**A P1 found by coverage triage, not by a report.** `for v in $(getcwd) { … }`
compiled clean and then killed the compiled program:
`sash: bug: bare command passed to sash_exec (expected absolute path)`, exit
127. All eight scalar value intrinsics, **both backends** — `--emit-c` emits
`const char* __t1_argv[] = { "getcwd", NULL }` in plain sight. `getenv` is the
same shape, masked by SB5020 (`--no-taint` confirms).

`try_dispatch_cmdsubst` rewrote **any** `$( )` for-in source into a pipeline
without looking inside; `resolve.rs::INTRINSICS` exempts intrinsic names from
DD#23 path resolution, presuming a downstream intrinsic lowering this path
never provided. **DD#111 documents the identical failure** for
`$(echo hi; status)` — the exemption is wider than the rewrite that justifies
it, and the for-in source was the second, still-open instance.

**DG generalised the fix**: "probably any for loop on a single scalar, quoted
or not, should be an error". So the rule is not "reject intrinsics here" but
**a for-in source must denote a collection** — a single scalar could only ever
run one iteration. `check_for_word` delegates to `for_source_scalar`, total
over `ExprKind` with the `do not add a wildcard` marker: the bug *was* a guard
keyed on one variant.

This closed the family's lone inconsistency. `ws.q1`-`ws.q3` already rejected
quoted *collections*, but `for v in "$s"` was accepted while `for v in $s` was
SB5009 — quoting a scalar *granted* it iteration. A literal word is still a
list (`for v in a b`, and `for v in a` degenerate); `$( )` splits on its
contents, a command being a line stream (DD#28/#40) and a value intrinsic a
scalar. `is_scalar_value_intrinsic` is derived from `INTRINSICS` minus
`argv`/`keys`.

**The sweep caught a spec I had not predicted.** Three casualties expected,
four arrived: `cov.173` asserted `for v in pre$s*post` globbed, but
`try_dispatch_glob` accepts only a bare `Literal`, never a `Concat`. The rule
was right; the spec pinned a shape the code never had. Found only by running
the sweep instead of trusting a grep.

New specs `fs.1`-`fs.9` in `control_flow.sh`; `fs.8`/`fs.9` guard over-reach.

**DG corrected two other conclusions of mine.** The `while read -r x` comment
in `try_dispatch_cmdsubst` described neither half of the code (the path emits
`SsaInst::ReadLine`; per DD#99 `readline` is scalar-per-line, `read` is
NUL-fields, and neither takes flags) — rewritten. And I had called
`magic_intrinsic_var`'s `"getpid" => "$"` mapping dead-by-construction and
proposed deleting the codegen arms it starves; DD#111 says the intrinsic **is
the real thing** and the parser is right to fold `$$` into `getpid`. The
transform unfolds it back.

**Next: reverse that desugar.** Keep `getpid`/`status`/`getcpid` canonical as
intrinsics through the transform so codegen's existing table arms lower them;
drop `magic_intrinsic_var`'s reverse mapping, `is_slotless_special`, and the
`"$"` special-cases in `codegen/values.rs` and `emit_c.rs`. That **closes** the
26 cold lines by making them live rather than deleting them — they were the
DD#111 violation visible as coverage, not dead code.

Then back to the coverage queue (`mk cov-union` first — this change renumbers
three measured files). Remaining cold: `lower_value_as_str_aggregate`,

`Scanner::header_depth` (mirroring `arith_depth`, set by `parse_compound_list`)

hardcoded-`1:1` guard would have been orphaned while all three sat green.
Added `dspan.4` (a stray `)`) to keep it covered.

Residual on record as `bc.g6`: `echo a { echo z }` (spaced) is still a command
plus a block where bash reads three literal words.

Filed `convert-brace-forms-passthrough` (P2) — `sash-convert` emits bash brace

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-30) — SB5067 extended to `$( … )` bodies ══

Sweep **7083** (3644 native, 3426 c, 13 skipped) — predicted exactly, zero
failures. `mk test`, fmt, clippy green. Journal 451.

**`q-cmdsub-body-taints-outer-global` is closed — DG chose (a).** The
net-effect rule now applies to anonymous bodies too. DD#86 already calls a
`$( … )` body an anonymous function body, and sash **inlines** it rather than
forking a subshell, so the write escapes; before this a function leaving a
global tainted was a located SB5067 and the identical `$( )` form was silent.

**It cost nothing.** The sweep's entire +12 is the six new dual-mode specs
(`bfb.23`-`bfb.28`); no existing spec changed verdict. The relaxation is what
made it affordable — the old objection was that (a) "would newly reject
programs that taint inside a body and attest after it", and under the
net-effect rule an adjacent **in-body** attest is the repair and already
worked. So the only newly-rejected shape is the leaky one the function rule
already rejected.

**DG deleted the exception I had flagged.** I had listed `:!` on a body-tainted
global as something the anonymous-function model leaves open. It is not: SB5067
fires at **body exit** and never examines the read site, so the bypass is
evaluated at a statement the rule has already failed before reaching. That also
retires the exception DG raised during the DD#121 discussion — the relaxation
had closed it weeks earlier as a side effect. `:!` still works where the intent
is local: a top-level taint, and a body's own locals.

**Architecturally it converts an assumption into a theorem.**
`taint_cmdsub_bodies`' clone-and-discard was sound for functions only because
SB5067 made the top level the only place a global's taint can arrive — the
invariant behind `taint_top_level`'s "no fixpoint". That now holds for bodies
too: the verdict makes the discarded set provably equal to the one the
enclosing scope keeps. Option (b) is closed with it.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-30) — SB5067 relaxed to a net-effect rule; SSA backstop now sees bulk fills ══

Sweep **7071** (3638 native, 3420 c, 13 skipped) — predicted exactly, zero
failures. `mk test` and fmt green. Journal 450.

DG's ruling on the open SB5067 question below was **"yes to (a) + (ii)"**. Both
landed.

**(a) SB5067 is now a net-effect rule.** A function body may not *exit* with a
global tainted that it did not *inherit* — replacing the old syntactic "may not
taint a global at all". DD#121 adjacency is what makes this safe: an attest
must immediately and unconditionally follow the taint, so a body can now taint
a global and clean it in the same breath. The bypass probe (top level taints,
attests clean, a function re-taints) is still rejected, because the attest
removed the name from the entry set and the re-taint is a net insert.

Not "clean at exit" — that is unsatisfiable. A body inherits the caller's set
and R1 forbids cleaning an inherited taint, so the first global tainted at top
level would put every function permanently in violation. Six specs
`bfb.17`-`bfb.22`; DD#121 addendum. Commit `fa18769`.

**(ii) the four bulk fills carry taint at SSA.** `ArgvFill`/`ReadArray`/
`SplitValue`/`MapFromArray` now define a real `VarRef` after the autodeclare,
so the layering is clean-declaration → tainted-fill → clean-attest and
`taint_of_name`'s max-version rule reads it correctly. Two prior passes
recorded that a `{array}_0` insert "did NOT work" without saying why; it never
could, because the empty autodeclare `Assign` is Clean at a *higher* version.
This also retires the "attest-clears check" the task file asked for — the
attest already defines a strictly higher clean version. Specs `sw.14`-`sw.19`.

**Two bugs it exposed, both fixed.** Giving the fills versions made
`load_var_or_empty` miss on `vars["a_2"]` — `map_inst_versioned` enumerated only
`Assign`/`ReadLine`/`CaptureEnd` — and that miss is *silent*: it returns a null
pointer, so `$(len a)` segfaulted. 53 specs at once. Same lesson as journal 449
in a new position: never create an SSA version defined on only one path. And
DD#60's rule that a length/count *measures* rather than reads was implemented
at the sink and in `cmd_subst_taint` but **not** in `value_is_tainted`, so the
verdict depended on which node the transform picked — live but unreachable
until a collection could be tainted (`via.12`). Both sides now share
`is_measurement_op`.

**Backstop bookkeeping.** `ssa-taint-full-backstop.md` gap 2 is closed and gap
3 was closed in journal 435. Gap 1 — capture-form builtins, whose taint is a
boolean fixed at transform time *before* analysis runs — is split out to
`notes/tasks/ssa-taint-capture-form-builtins.md`. DG's 2026-09-12 deferral
condition still holds: every shape there is SB5020 under a normal compile.

**Open for DG.** Reusing the number SB5067 for the relaxed rule was my call
(it keeps all seven existing spec assertions structurally valid) — reported,
not ruled on. `q-cmdsub-body-taints-outer-global` remains yours; its option (a)

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-30) — P1 SIGSEGV fixed; the crash was non-reproducible codegen ══

Sweep **7034** (3626 native, 3408 c, 13 skipped) — predicted exactly, zero
failures. `mk test`, fmt, clippy green. Journal 449.

**`bug-caught-attest-all-fail-path-undefined-handle` is closed**, and the
filing's own diagnosis was wrong in a way worth remembering. It recorded the
crash as depending on "process memory layout" and prescribed reproducing under
`env P=x`. The ritual worked, which is why nobody questioned it.

It was **compile-time** nondeterminism. One unchanged source compiled to two
different binaries — `7c6a03c9` faulted, `131fb478` did not. `env` never
perturbed anything; it rode along with whichever binary that compile produced.
The tell was that `then/fi` crashed and `{ }` did not, for a program where the
two spellings parse identically.

**Root cause.** `codegen::types::find_array_slot` resolved a collection by name
via `vars.keys().find(…)` — an arbitrary `HashMap` key. The only producer of a
second `a_*` key is `emit_attest_retag`, which materialised DD#61's
clean-retag as fresh Cranelift vars defined in the **pass block only**. On the
failing path that key existed with no definition, and a coin-flip decided
whether `sash_table_len` got it. `--emit-c` never faulted — c has always
treated `AttestRetag` as a no-op — which localised it to native in one step.

The filing's "undefined phi edge" guess was wrong in mechanism: there is no
phi, and `lower_if_attest`'s pre-state restore at the merge is correct.

**Fixed both halves.** `emit_attest_retag` now *aliases* the target version to
the same `VarSlot` (a compile-time relabelling must not create a runtime
value); `find_array_slot`'s fallback is deterministic — the lowest version,
generalising the `_0`-first rule already above it. Reproducible output restored.

**The pin took three tries.** `join`/`len` never reproduce it (they do not use
`find_array_slot`); only a splat read does. And one compile caught it ~60% of
the time, so `sw.12` compiles **six times** on purpose. Verified it fails 3/3
against the original code — a gate that cannot fail is not a gate.

**Open for DG: SB5067.** Still in place, and measurement sharpened the picture.
Dropping it wholesale is unsound, but today's rule over-rejects: it fires on
the taint *unconditionally*, so it also rejects
`fn f { g=$(getenv X); attest g [[ … ]] }`, which DD#121 makes provably safe.
The only genuine hole left is a bulk-filled global **collection** read without
an attest — scalars are already caught by SB5020 / the SSA backstop.
Recommended replacement: a body-exit rule ("a function may not *leave* a global
tainted"), a strict relaxation that keeps all 7 existing specs and needs no
fixpoint. Not actioned — DG's call.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-30) — DD#121: attest must be adjacent ══

Sweep **7030** (3624 native, 3406 c, 13 skipped) — predicted exactly, zero
failures. `mk test` green. Journal 448.

**DG's thesis, measured and ratified.** *"Requiring attest to immediately and
unconditionally follow the operation that taints a variable eliminates all
order-dependent taint-bypass. Absent an attest, the tainted variable can only
be read with `:!`."* The second clause was already shipped law (SB5020 rejects
every read form; DD#91's `:!` is the bypass). The first is now **DD#121**.

- **R1 adjacency — SB5088.** An `attest` clears taint only as the immediately
  following statement, in the same block, of the one that tainted its subject.
- **R2 caught resolution — SB5089.** `if attest` / `attest … &&` / `attest …
  ||` must leave the subject clean on every path that **falls through**.
  `exit`/`return`/`break`/`continue` are exempt; `else :` is not. The no-else
  form is rejected, which supersedes DD#24's `attest … && CMD` row.
- **R3** unchanged: `:!` remains the per-use bypass.

**Why it was worth it.** `attest` was a statement that *removed* a name from a
mutable set at an arbitrary program point. That single property caused all
three P1 filings — it breaks joins, breaks the call-graph fixpoint (the only
reason SB5067 exists), and creates "at which program point do I read the set?".
The set is now grow-only and taint is ordinary reaching-definitions.

**Two P1s closed, both verified rejected rather than assumed:**
`bug-attest-in-branch-leaks-past-merge` (the leak was *every* block form — if,
while, and zero-trip for) and `bug-slot-inward-taint-reads-final-set`.

**Implementation added three things the DD did not anticipate**, all found by
running specs — see journal 448. Briefly: a whole-variable assignment from a
clean RHS now **kills** taint (R2 is unsatisfiable otherwise); adjacency has
four *structural* positions (a `while`/`if` condition, a `for` in-source, and
DD#100 slot arrival, each heading the block below it); and the effect of a
statement must be measured against an **empty** set, or a re-taint of an
already-tainted name looks like a no-op.

**Cost:** 20 spec rewrites, every one a single added `else`. Ten new specs
`bfb.7`-`bfb.16`.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-30) — every disposition default is a literal ══

Sweep **7023** (3614 native, 3396 c, 13 skipped) — predicted exactly, zero
failures; the purge announced exactly the 14 retirements I made. `mk test`,
fmt, clippy, totality green. Journal 447.

**DG went a step past the filing.** Journal 446 ended by noting that the
eagerness `:-`'s rules were built to contain was never a safety decision — just
pre-existing branchless-select codegen. DG: "the `:-` default, let's change it
to match the `:?` so eager/side-effects are a non-issue."

So **all three** disposition defaults take a literal operand — `${x:-D}`,
`@{a:-D}`, `$(arg N D)` — with `$` rejected as SB4070 unless the whole operand
is single-quoted. A conditionally-taken operand raises "when is this evaluated"
and "what may it do"; a literal raises neither.

**Deleted, all of it answering one of those two questions:** SB5035 and its
four helpers (`flag_random_default`, `random_default_diag`,
`expr_invokes_random`, `cmdsub_head_is`); DD#78's read discipline on `:-`
(`check_param_expansion_taint` walks no operand now); the hybrid eager/lazy
lowering (`lift_default_value` is a branchless select again, `contains_capture`
gone) and its specs `lift.4`-`lift.10`. The taint hole DD#78 Stage 1 closed is
still closed — by the grammar rather than by a checker that must stay total.

**One rule, two implementations, on purpose.** `${ }`/brace-less are rejected
in the parser *textually* (DG's spec read literally: any `$` unless
single-quoted). `$(arg N D)` cannot be — nothing knows a word belongs to `arg`
until validate — so it is rejected there *structurally*, via a new
`first_expansion` walker (total over `ExprKind`, totality-gated). The
single-quote escape falls out free: `SingleQuoted` holds no expansion.

**Out of scope by design:** `${x:s/RE/SUB/}` stays a full interpolating word.
It is a *pattern*, evaluated unconditionally, so neither question arises.
`parse_interpolating_word` (was `parse_default_word`) survives for it alone —
and `cov.223`/`224`/`225` moved their vehicle there, reaching the same scanner
arms.

**Expressiveness loss, recorded not rediscovered:** a literal `}` in a default
is unrepresentable (`$'a\x7db'` contains `$`; the brace scanner is pure
depth-matching so quotes do not protect a `}`). Already true of `:?`. Pinned by
`vm.dv2`.

DD#65's follow-on carries the rule; DD#78's final amendment records that it
**retains no live rule** and is kept for the account;
`q-sb5035-random-ban-vestigial` is resolved by deletion.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-30) — `$` in a `:?` abort message is SB4070 ══

Sweep **7037** (3621 native, 3416 c, 13 skipped) — predicted exactly, zero
failures. `mk test`, fmt, clippy, totality green. Journal 446.

**I made an abort message run user code, and DG caught it by asking.** The
previous session read DD#78's Scope clause as authority to parse `${x:?MESSAGE}`
as an interpolating word. DD#78 groups `:-` and `:?` by *purpose* — a purity
rule on the operand; the **parse** is DD#65's, and the interpolating-word
spelling is `:-`'s alone. DG: "`:?` is an abort. The code is exiting. Treating
MESSAGE as an interpolating word means more code can run."

Measured, it was worse than a style question. `${y:?$(g)}` forked and exec'd
`g` **on the path where `y` was set and no abort happened** — the message is
materialized eagerly. Exit 0, no output, user code ran. And `$(( ))` is a call
site too (DD#58's arith sexpr), so "ban `$( )` but keep the word" is not a
rule that can be stated.

**Reverting was half a fix, twice.** `@{a:?WORD}` had *always* been the more
permissive spelling and stayed a call site after the scalar revert; and a bare
literal degrades silently — `${y:?$m}` quietly emitting `$m` is the SB4047
failure. So: **SB4070**, `$` rejected unless the whole message is `'…'`-wrapped
(quotes stripped, `$` kept), at both spellings via one `parse_abort_message`.

DD#65 carries the rule, DD#78's `${x:?MESSAGE}` scope clause is **withdrawn**
(Stage 1 of that same DD had said "nothing to check" — it disagreed with
itself), and `bug-require-message-not-interpolated` records that its own fix
was wrong and voids its gates.

**Open, from DG's "perhaps `:-` should be simplified":**
`q-sb5035-random-ban-vestigial` — **resolved the next day** by making every
disposition default a literal; SB5035 is deleted outright. See the entry above.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-29) — taint walks substitution bodies ══

Sweep **7027** (3616 native, 3411 c, 13 skipped) — predicted exactly.
`mk test`, fmt, clippy, totality green. Journal 445.

**`check_taint` never walked the statements inside a `$( … )` body.** The one
function that looked inside matched `if let StmtKind::Command`, so a
Declaration / If / While / Redirected statement was skipped, and it measured
reads against the OUTER tainted set, which never holds a body-defined name.
Between them, nothing in a body was checked: a tainted value could reach a
redirect target, a test operand or a builtin argument and get only the SSA
backstop's message — no SB code, no span.

`taint_stmt` now descends unconditionally into `cmdsub_bodies()`. That is the
**third** time this session one bug shape has appeared — `validate_stmt_ctx`,
then `check_stmt`/`infer_stmt`, now `taint_stmt`. Every one of those
dispatchers reached its body helper from the `_` arm, and the arms that carry a
substitution are the *leaves*. Widening `_` reaches none of them.

**Two measurements worth keeping.** `check_cmdsub_inner_reads` looked redundant
once the descent landed; stubbing it failed 12 specs x 2 modes, so it is
load-bearing for expression-walk positions and was kept. And the 20 sweep
failures were all specs using a `$( )` body as a *vehicle*: `bkstp.1`-`bkstp.12`
moved to `taint_switch.sh` under `--no-taint-cst`, which is now the only way to
reach the backstop at all; `av.c5`, `av.c6`, `csc.16` were reading `argv` output
unattested and were passing only because bodies went unchecked.

Specs `cbt.1`-`cbt.10` assert the SB code **and** the `:LINE:COL:` span, which
is what distinguishes the new diagnostic from the backstop it replaces.

**Open for DG:** should a `$( )` body that taints an outer global be SB5067,
as a function body is? The write persists at runtime, the taint does not
follow, and `taint_top_level`'s no-fixpoint invariant depends on the answer.
Filed as `q-cmdsub-body-taints-outer-global` with both options measured.

**Remaining open bugs:** `bug-brace-breaks-unquoted-word` (P2, needs DG — three
options, one may collide with brace expansion) and
`bug-match-3arg-in-cmdsub-rejected` (P4, wording only).

## 2026-09-29 — the type pass had the same hole, and it was uncovered

Cleared the last filing from the `$( )` thread,

except inside a capture body.

per body "copying `check_function`" — but `check_function` opens no child

fixed earlier the same day; the arms that carry a substitution are the leaves.

An entire pass was switched on over a class of statements and nothing moved,
which says the suite had no coverage of type-checking inside a body at all.
That is what `csc.35`-`csc.40` are for, mirroring `csc.31`-`csc.34` on the type
side: `validate` reaching a body says nothing about `type_check` reaching it.

all green. DD#86 addendum, journal 444c.

**All five filings from the `$( )` thread are now closed or corrected.** Next

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-29) — forty-two of forty-five ══

Sweep **6948 passing, 13 skipped, zero failing** (6961 total — the predicted
+48: 24 specs × 2 modes). `mk test` green. fmt, clippy, totality and the
complexity gate all clean. Journal 444. **DD#86 amended.**

A dropped statement in a `for`-in header turned into a structural change to
how the compiler recurses.

`validate.rs::cmdsub_command_is` decided what a `$( … )` *was* from
`stmts.first()` and a command name. So `for x in $(argv; /usr/bin/touch F)`
compiled clean, looped correctly, and never created `F`; and DD#60's two
`argv` shapes — the splat expression `$(argv N)` and the out-param fill
statement `argv N a` — were indistinguishable, so the fill was rejected with a
diagnostic telling the author to write what they had written. **DG chose (a):
the fill is legal inside a body**, because it is a statement and DD#86 makes a
body a function body.

**Fixing that exposed the next one.** `resolve_single_cmdsubst` returned
`Option` and `None` was read as "external, so exec it". Sixteen statement
builtins have no value lowering — `:`, `write`, `cd`, `wait`, `close`,
`attest`, `unset`, the `argv` fill — so each, as the sole body, printed
`sash: bug: bare command passed to sash_exec` into the program's own stdout
and exited **0**.

**And that exposed the third.** `$(signal INT ignore)` still panicked the
compiler; `$(mapfile -m q)` still ICEd at runtime; `$(break)`,
`$(read -a "q")` and `$(for args in …)` were still accepted in silence. Each
traced to a *different* pass, so I asked the index how general it was:

> **42 of the 45 `child_bodies()` walkers in `validate.rs` had no cmdsub
> descent.**

Body *expressions* were reachable through `walk_expr_tree`; body *statements*
were not, because `child_bodies()` did not yield them. That asymmetry is the
bug class, and it constrains the fix — adding statement coverage without
removing the expression route doubles every expression diagnostic (journal
308). I gave DG three shapes with that number attached; **he chose the
structural move**.

`child_bodies()` is now `structural_bodies()` ++ `cmdsub_bodies()`, and
`walk_expr_tree` stops at `CommandSubstitution`. A body belongs to exactly one
side of the recursion. The classification rule, now in DD#86: **a pass with
its own `CommandSubstitution` arm keeps it and takes `structural_bodies()`; a
pass without one takes `child_bodies()` and gets the body for free.** A pass
that mutates scope state is pinned regardless until it opens a child scope.

**The suite did not catch the regression I introduced.** `validate_stmt_ctx`'s
leaf arms never recurse, and pre-change `walk_own_exprs_in_stmt` had reached
body expressions by descending *through* the substitution node. Moving bodies
took that away, and `$RANDOM`, `$HOME` and `**` inside a body compiled clean
for one build — past 6913 green rows. It surfaced only because I wrote a spec
for a bug I believed was already fixed and the compiler still panicked.
csc.34 is now the duplication guard: SB5017 exactly **once** at depth three.

The complexity gate rejected six functions — two I had materially changed,
four pre-existing violators whose only edit was the one-token
`child_bodies` → `structural_bodies` substitution. All six were the same
shape, a nested double loop inside a match arm. Flattened; all green.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-28) — the rule that only needed asking once ══

Sweep **6874 passing, 13 skipped, zero failing** (6887 total — the predicted
+22: 11 specs × 2 modes). `mk test` 71/27/20. fmt, clippy, totality, all
gates clean. Journal 443. **DD#84 and DD#100 amended.**

I had left DG three options on the arity bug. He answered with a rule that
made all three moot:

> an elision, given it could remove an argument, can only work for a variadic
> context and not a fixed one. similarly, a splat should only work for
> variadic given it could be empty

**The section of my filing that argued against it was invented.** I claimed
the rule kills DD#84's motivating case, `f a ${maybe:~}` into a `Fixed{1,2}`
callee. DD#84 never promised that — it says an absent optional arg is one
*"known at compile time"*, which a `:~` elide by construction is not. I
asserted it from reading the DD's intent rather than its text, in the same
file whose own 2026-09-17 addendum records exactly that failure against
itself. A second claim in the filing — that bare `@a` is rejected at a call
site — is false and has been gated as legal by spec sp.1 since September.

**Measured cost of the rule: one spec out of 6865.** I reasoned my way to
"this breaks a documented feature" about a change I could have measured in
ten minutes, and did measure within ten minutes of accepting it.

Implemented as **SB5087**: a splat or elide may go only where the callee
takes any number, and only when the call's minimum meets that callee's floor.
Static calls keep their SB5042/SB5043 messages verbatim.

**DG then tightened the variadic half.** A variadic callee can still read an
index bare, and I first checked that floor by *summing* per-argument minimums.
He gave the model — "the fixed met by discrete arguments as though there were
no variadic component" — and summing does not meet it: `f @e x` reached a
floor of 1 as `0 + 1`, and `${args[0]}` then read `x` on an empty `e` and
`e[0]` otherwise. A fixed read silently taking a different variable's value
depending on an array length, with nothing said at compile time. The check now
walks *positions* and stops at the first variable-length argument. Zero
existing specs affected; 84.68-84.72.

It also makes DD#84 uniform: its three "elidable positions" are all variadic
contexts. A user-function call is the fourth, elidable iff the callee is
variadic. The closed list was the rule minus the one position with an arity.

**Then the rule turned over three more bugs**, because implementing it meant
knowing what a splat lowers to at all four call positions — and three of them
did not lower it at all:

- **The pipeline stage joined.** `f @two | cat` fused `"a b"` and `"c"` into
  one argument. This is `bug-splat-to-user-function-joins`, fixed and marked
  `done` on 2026-09-10, in a third position its fix never visited — journal
  441's "second implementation", now the third, of the same function.
- **`=name` reached its slot on one path in four.** `split_call_args` had one
  caller. Elsewhere `=q` lowered as a scalar: silent wrong answer in a
  pipeline, **SIGSEGV** in a string capture, **ICE** in an `-> int` capture.
  SB5050 masked it — twice now — until I added an independent read.
- **Two validate scans skipped `$( )` entirely**, so DD#100's scalars-first
  rule was not checked inside a capture at all: `str t=$(f =q "x")` compiled.
- **`: @args` promoted optional args to required.** `analyze_arity`'s
  variadic floor chained `required ∪ optional`; the marker that widens
  arity was narrowing it.

Specs: `optional_args.sh` 84.53–84.67, `collparam.sh` 100.38–100.45,
`functions.sh` sp.9–sp.11, sp.3 migrated. Both task files closed; the stale

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-28) — counting is not accessing ══

Sweep **6822 passing, 13 skipped, zero failing** (6835 total — the predicted
+26: 13 specs × 2 modes). Zero flips vs `5d15780`, nothing retired. `mk test`
71/27/20 unchanged. All gates clean. Journal 442. **DD#81 amended.**

DG read the arity bug I filed at the end of 441 and said the example
functions were not variadic — "the use of len alone shouldn't qualify".

**The filing was wrong, and I had pasted the proof.** Both reproducers used
`int n=$(len args)`, which DD#81 Part B made a whole-args read, so the callee
was `Variadic{floor:2}` — while the file's prose called it `Fixed{min:2}`.
Three lines down sat the diagnostic I had quoted: *"expects **at least** 2
arguments"*. "At least" is the variadic message. I copied a compiler error
into a document to support a claim it contradicted and did not read it.

Rewritten against a genuinely fixed-arity callee (`83c1953`); both directions
still reproduce, now with the messages agreeing. New detail: a three-element
splat also reports "called with 1", so the count is the constant 1 for *any*
splat.

**Then DG settled the rule underneath it.** I checked `notes/decisions/`
first, reported that `len → variadic` was deliberate (DD#81 Part B, stated
three times, accepted 2026-08-25), measured the cost of changing it at 17
specs, and asked. His answer:

> `$(len args)` is how a function would loop over variadic args; but
> accessing an arg via a loop or branch is what would make it variadic.
> Without the loop/branch the len is vacuous.

`len` is the *loop bound*; the **access** inside the loop — a dynamic index —
is what `analyze_arity` should key on, and already did independently. So the
old rule carried no signal and cost a ceiling: one mention of `$#` or
`$(len args)` anywhere in a body turned `Fixed{2,2}` into "any count", and
`f p d x y` into a two-argument function printed `4 [p][d]`, silently
discarding two arguments.

Verified before believing it: every real variadic idiom survives on its own
access (dynamic index, `@args`, `$(join args)`, and DD#84's `${args[1]:-}`).
All 17 failing specs pulled up and read — **all 17 are count-without-access**
(`echo $#`, `$(( $# * 2 ))`, `if (( $# < 2 ))`, `${arr[$#]}`). Not one is a
variadic loop.

The recovery was already in the language, and the error already pointed at
it: DD#81's no-op `: @args`, which SB5043 names in its own text — "use @args
to accept a variable number".

Two compiler lines, the DD#81 addendum, 17 specs migrated, 13 new
(81.17–81.29) covering both halves of the rule.

**Not changed:** DG said "loop **or** branch". A conditionally-read *literal*
index stays a required fixed index — DD#84's `${args[1]:-}` → `Fixed{1,2}`
already states that optionality, and taking "branch" literally would swap a
two-sided bound for none. Flagged in the DD and to DG.

**Still open for DG:** `bug-call-arity-counts-compile-time-values` (P1) — the
A/B/C call on a runtime arity shortfall. Unaffected by the above; its
reproducers carry no count.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-28) — the second implementation ══

Sweep **6796 passing, 13 skipped, zero failing** (6809 total — the predicted
+46: 23 specs × 2 modes). Zero flips. `mk test` 71 unchanged. All gates clean.

Three bugs, one sentence for all three: **a compile-time count taken over a
value that only exists at runtime.** Two fixed, one open for DG.

**1. DD#84 elidability is an allowlist now — and the DD already said so.**
I had filed the eleven elision ICEs as a language question for DG. It was
not one. DD#84's "Elidable positions" is a closed three-item list, and the
middle one is "a `sash`-**varargs** builtin arg list" — which excludes every

allow-by-default, with the two exceptions that had been *reported*, each
appended after it panicked. Six of the suite's thirteen SB5046 specs are
regressions for this one bug. Now total over `BuiltinCmd`, no wildcard.

> A denylist whose failure mode is a compiler panic will be patched forever,
> once per report.

**2. `exec` had its own argv builder in BOTH backends, and it was hiding a
silent truncation.** `exec` is legitimately elidable — its args are an
external command's argument list — so I went to find why it panicked, and
found `build_argv_on_stack`, a stale copy of `build_argv_fixed` sitting fifty
lines from its only caller. Missing line: `emit_argv_guard`. So DD#99 stage 7
did not apply, and `exec cmd "$s"` with an interior NUL **truncated at execve
and exited 0** — the callee got a shorter argument than the program had
validated. The c backend had the same duplication and the same two ICEs, but
*did* emit the guard, so the oracle would have caught it the moment a spec
existed. `exec` had no splat, elide, or NUL coverage at all.

> Cross-backend agreement is only evidence when the two were built
> independently. Here each was a copy of the same omission, and the doc
> comment recorded that as parity.

**3. Open for DG — SB5042/SB5043 count compile-time SsaValues.** Both
directions wrong. `f one ${x:~}` with empty `x` delivers **argc=1** to a
callee the compiler itself calls `Fixed{min:2}` — writing `f one` literally
is SB5042. And `f @q` with a two-element `q` into a `Fixed{2,2}` callee is
*rejected*, "called with 1", a count true of no execution.

The fix is a range check; what it does not settle is the overlap case. The
tempting fail-closed answer (reject dynamic counts into fixed-arity callees)
kills DD#84's own motivating case — "pass a second arg if I have one" against
a `Fixed{1,2}` callee is always in range. Options A/B/C with a lean toward B
(emit a runtime check) in
`notes/tasks/bug-call-arity-counts-compile-time-values.md`.

> A second implementation is not redundancy. It is a place where one of the
> two will be improved and the other will not, and nothing reports it.

**The SB5031 splat bug is fixed, and there was no decision to make.** I filed
it as DG's call — a false rejection traded against a false acceptance. Asked to
explain the decision, I measured the direction I had only reasoned about:

```sh
fn f { array a=(1 2); /bin/echo @{a:-z}; }
f
/bin/echo @{a:-z}          # accepted, and printed `1 2`
```

DD#86 makes that name local to `f`, and the `$y` / `$a[0]` spellings of the
same read both reject. Only the splat leaked, at runtime. So the flat
`program_scopes` union was not conservative — it was wrong in both directions,
and the tradeoff did not exist.

**Why the other spellings were right.** The main SB5031 check is scope-aware:
`check_reads_in_scope` threads `known` per scope and descends into `$( )`
bodies, so DD#86's worked example rejects and the in-body read accepts.
`validate.rs` says the sink exists so read-checks "can never diverge on what
counts as a read". `check_scalar_splat` was bolted on later, beside that
traversal rather than into it, and is the one that diverged.

**The fix.** A splat now records through `ReadSink::record_splat` against the
current scope's `known`. The reason it fell through before is worth keeping: a
disposition is an *operator*, and `record_param` treats any operator as
SB5031's opt-out — which is right for `${x:-…}` and wrong for `@{a:-z}`, where
the disposition covers the array being **empty**, not **undeclared**.
`check_scalar_splat` keeps SB5079 only. Nothing needed widening; the
scope-aware traversal already went everywhere the answer lives.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-28) — P0: a heap pointer reaches argv ══

Found while answering DG's question about how a `$( )` body is validated. It
has nothing to do with command substitution — that was only the path that
removed the masking.

```sh
argv x
attest e in x [[ -n $e ]]
/bin/echo $x        # 0x7f3ce6cc2040 — a live mmap address, fresh each run
```

`read x` is the same. **Both backends produce it identically**, so it is the
shared model, not a codegen divergence. The emitted C is four lines:
`x_ptr = (const char*)__t0_tbl; x_len = 0;` puts the table in the *scalar*
slot, then `sash_argv_guard(x_ptr, x_len)` is handed length 0 and validates
nothing while `execve` reads to the first NUL — through the table header,
whose first field is a pointer. It also propagates: `str y=$x` carries it into
an ordinary scalar.

**Two collection sets that disagree.** `type_check.rs` registers auto-declared
targets in `env.collections` (`register_argv_target`, `register_newread_target`
— the DD#60/DD#61 auto-declare). `validate.rs::collect_collection_names` walks
only `StmtKind::Declaration` with `-a`/`-A`. SB5064 — the guard written for
exactly this spelling — consults the incomplete one, so `array x=(a);
/bin/echo $x` is correctly rejected and `argv x; … /bin/echo $x` is not.

Second fault, independent: auto-declare never checks for a conflicting
declaration, though the explicit form does. `str x=safe; array x=(a)` is
SB5049; `str x=safe; read x` silently retypes, and `int x=1; read x` is
`ICE: expected string var, got int`. The `map` case is caught only by accident,
via attest-all's binder arity.

Masked all along by the guards that fire first — SB5020 on the untainted
spelling, SB5050 on the short ones, SB4018 on `matchall`. The leak is reachable
only *after* you satisfy them, which is why no spec found it.

**Not fixed — two questions for DG.** Where the single collection set should
live (the recomputed-worse-view is the cause), and whether `str x=…; read x`
should be SB5049 like `array x=(a)`, or a sanctioned rebind. The `int` ICE must
stop either way.
→ `notes/tasks/bug-autodeclared-collection-scalar-read-leaks-pointer.md`

### What the question actually was: how is a `$( )` body compiled?

Answered, and worth recording because the model is not what the code comments
say. **Codegen does exactly the recursive lowering DG expected** — the body's
statements go through `lower_stmts` into ordinary blocks of the *same* SSA
function (`_blk_1: /* cap_body */`), with no fork when the body is pure.
Isolation is then re-imposed deliberately: `capture_body_into`
(`transform/stmt_handlers.rs:1307`) snapshots every variable the body assigns
and restores it after (`__save_bodycap_x`). So there is no subshell — there is
a compiler-synthesized save/restore, and the comments calling it "subshell
isolation" are describing the effect, not the mechanism.

**Validate is the one layer that does not recurse.** Positionals (SB5024),
elide (SB5046), argv-splat (SB5025), resolve and type-check all walk the body.
Taint alone substitutes `check_cmdsub_inner_reads` — four lines, `if let
StmtKind::Command`, only `c.args` and collection readers, and it never records
a definition. That is the whole of the P1 escape filed earlier.

And the save/restore is itself not total: `collect_assigned_into`
(`stmt_handlers.rs:1359`) handles `Assignment` and `Declaration` only, so a
subscript assignment leaks out of the body (`a[0]=leaked` survives) and so does
a builtin write. Against DG's model — no subshells, writes survive unless a
fork is required — the open question is whether the leak or the restore is the
part that is wrong.

### Landed: `$(int x=1)` is no longer "unterminated `$(`"

`)` is `Tok::RParen`, and DD#71 absorb makes it a literal in an assignment
value — so `int x=1)` ate the substitution's own terminator and the body ran to
end of input. SB4057 was telling the truth about what the parser saw. The tell
was in plain sight all along: top-level `int y=1)` is SB4030 "cannot assign
**string** value to int variable `y`".

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-28) — the lift was not total; `:-` is now lazy ══

Working the coverage queue head (`lower_value_as_str_aggregate` — six cold
lines, all deliberate ICE guards) into the useful question, "is any of these
arms actually reachable", turned up a live one.

`lift_int_func_calls` materializes every nested `$(f)` capture into a temp,
because an unlifted `FuncCall` reaching codegen is an ICE by construction. It
covered six of `SsaValue`'s thirty-one variants and ended `other => other,
// no IntFuncCall inside`. That comment was the bug: `other` was fifteen more
variants, most of which own sub-values.

```sh
array a=( $(f) )        map m=([k]=$(f))        str z=${arr[$(f)]}
str z=${y:-$(f)}        a[0]=${y:-$(f)}
```

All valid bash; all crashed the compiler. `str z=$(f)` — the same capture not
nested inside anything — worked, which is why it survived. The walk is now
**total over `SsaValue` with no wildcard** (cc 26 / cog 1, dispatcher
exemption), and `handle_subscript_assign` — which never called the lift at all
— now lifts both operands.

**The third non-total match in three sessions** (journal 430's walker pair,
431's `Trusted` wrap, this). The convention holds: make it total, say so in the
doc comment, let the compiler enforce it.

### DG's call: `:-` lowers lazily

`DefaultValue` was not mechanical, because `:-` is lazy — bash evaluates the
operand only when the fallback fires. Recursing eagerly hoists the capture and
runs `f` unconditionally. DG chose **lower lazily** over lift-eagerly or
reject.

**DD#78 had already chosen eager, and its premise was wrong.** It argues eager
is safe because every legal default is side-effect-free — then lists **user
functions** among the allowed defaults. A user function is not side-effect-free
in any enforced sense. Nobody noticed because the compiler *ICEd* on exactly
that construct: the allowance was dead letter, and no spec in the suite
exercised it. Amended, not reversed — captureless defaults stay eager (every
operand the original reasoning contemplated), only a capture-bearing one gets
control flow. Built in transform, so neither backend grew a special case and
DD#78's "avoids per-backend branching" cost is not paid.

### Gates

Sweep predicted 6661, returned 6661 — zero failing, zero flips. `lift.1`-`.12`
in `spec/functions.sh`, each verified against bash first, each landed by one of
six disjoint neuters. `lift.6` is the sole laziness witness and must be: with
the operand hoisted it still prints `[set]`, so only the untaken `f`'s stderr
catches it.

### Filed, not fixed

`${x:?MESSAGE}` is emitted as **literal source text** — sash prints `$(f)`,
bash prints `hi`. DD#78 names the message as a checked read position; it is not
one (`${y:?$h}` with `h` tainted gives **SB5050 dead-variable**, not SB5020 —
the operand is not in the value graph at all). Not a taint leak, since nothing
is expanded and so nothing escapes. → `notes/tasks/bug-require-message-not-interpolated.md`

Also checked and **correct, leave alone**: the many `DD#77` comments on
`RequireValue`. DD#77 §"`:?` un-prune scope" re-added scalar `:?` after DD#65
pruned it; DD#65's "rejected for SCALAR" line is the stale one.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-27) — DD#91: `!` is scoped to its own read ══

DG answered the question journal 430 filed rather than prejudged:

> "x=$(getenv A); y=$(getenv B); z=$x:!-$y:! ; the `!` should only apply to the
> read of the variable's stored value"

**The ruling made his own example a bug report.** `parameter_expansion_to_value`
wrapped the subject in `SsaValue::Trusted` only in the no-operator arm; the
moment there was an operator, `source_carrying_value` built `DefaultValue` and
never looked at `taint_off`. So the `!` of **every** `${x:!-…}` reached neither
backend nor backstop, and even the fully-vouched `${x:!-${y:!}}` failed to
compile — on the unspanned SSA backstop.

Three validate sites had the mirror-image fault, treating `taint_off` as
covering the whole expansion including its default: `is_taint_source`
(`!pe.taint_off &&`), `pexp_uses_tainted` and `check_param_expansion_taint`
(early returns that skipped the `:-` operand walk too).

A fourth was self-inflicted: `source_is_int` matches `Var`/`Subscript`
**structurally**, so the new wrapper silently moved `${n:!-7}` off the int
identity-element path. `!` is a taint annotation, not a change of type — it now
sees through `Trusted`. A set non-zero int cannot detect this (both paths return
42); the probe has to be `n=0`.

**Three of five neuters landed nothing on the first pass.** N2 was the vacuous
42. N3/N4 were masked by N5 — in scalar position `check_param_expansion_taint`
rejects first, so the `reject_tainted_into_array` walker pair needed collection
position (`array a=( ${h:!-$p} )`), and `is_taint_source` needed a *source*
rather than a tainted variable because the `||` short-circuits. All five now
land disjoint specs.

**DD#90 rule 5 left as-is, on DG's call.** `$x:!-$y:!` still does not work: the
inner `$y:!` inside an operand is `$y` + literal `:!`, because the operand is an
interpolating parts list. Asked whether to extend brace-less into the operand,
DG: *"I'd actually use attest, so avoid over-indexing on taint-bypass
ergonomics."* Now pinned deliberately — vm.bl24 asserts the silent `abc:!`,

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-27) — TAINT ESCAPE closed (DD#61) ══

Chasing a coverage queue item (`test_uses_tainted`, 7 cold lines) found an
exploitable taint escape. Journal 430.

**The bug.** SB5021 is decided by `is_taint_source(e) || expr_uses_tainted(e,
tainted)` — two walkers read as a pair, which between them must cover the
whole tree. `expr_uses_tainted` was made total in journal 400 and carries a
long comment saying a wildcard leaked three times. **Its twin kept the
`_ => false` that comment is about.** Wherever the twin descended and this did
not, a *source* was invisible to both: the first never arrived, the second
arrived asking a different question.

```sh
str x=""
array a=(q)
a[0]=${x:-$(</tmp/secret)}     # compiled CLEAN — no SB5021, no backstop
echo "${a[0]}"                 # …and printed the file
```

Also `$(getenv …)` and external captures; also via `[[ ]]` read-back, which
journal 400 already recorded escapes the SSA backstop entirely. A tainted
*variable* in the identical position (`${x:-$t}`) was SB5021 throughout —
which is what made it a hole rather than a policy.

**A second hole**, found by the differential: `str z=${b[$(getenv N)]}` was
clean while `echo "${b[$(getenv N)]}"` was SB5020. `reject_scalar_rhs_read`'s
subscript arm says *"the container AND the index are both reads"* and then
checked the index with the **value** walker. The code contradicted its comment.

**Fixed** by making all three walkers in the family total —
`is_taint_source`, `check_value_cmdsub_reads` (it had the same `_ => {}`), and
the index arm of `reject_scalar_rhs_read`. `Subscript` stays false in
`is_taint_source` on purpose (the index is a read, not the stored value).
`Test` stays a correct recursive answer rather than an ICE — unlike journal
429's `:~` arm, nothing *guarantees* its deadness, and this bug is the proof
that such arms become reachable.

**Open for DG:** does DD#91's `!` vouch for a *source* materialised in a `:-`

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-27) — coverage: function number was wrong by 36 points ══

Answering "what is current coverage" surfaced a bug in `contrib/covdb.py`.
`cov_lines` and `cov_branches` are keyed on things that mean the same in every
build, so they merge correctly across the two builds spliced into
`union.lcov`. `cov_fns` was keyed on `(file, mangled)` — and a Rust v0 mangled
name embeds the **crate disambiguator hash**, which differs between the spec
binary and the unit-test harness. Every function got two rows, one per build,
and the build that did not reach it contributed a permanent zero.

`emit_arith_op` read `count=0` while its own lines were 21/23 covered. Fixed
by stripping the build hashes before keying. **Deliberately not** keyed on
`(file, line)` like `cov_lines`: that gives a better-looking 98.7% and is
wrong, because closures share a start line with their parent and ~574 symbols
would merge — the same class of error, in the flattering direction.

**Only wrong since 2026-09-24, and by a commit that never touched the
counting.** `covdb.py` was introduced defaulting to the *spec-only*
`branch.lcov` — one build, one crate hash, correct. `b4981d7` switched the
default to `union.lcov` for a good reason (the 100% target is spec ∪ unit),
did not touch the keying, and thereby broke it. A key that had been unique
became per-build. Every figure we have ever *quoted* — 98.45% back to
95.03% — came from `cargo llvm-cov report`'s own summary via `mk cov`, which
reads the covmap and never an lcov, so the two numbers share no code path.

It survived because nothing consumes `cov_fns`; the documented triage query
ranks uncovered *lines* by function and was always correct. A number with no
consumer is a number with no test.

Union coverage of `sash/src` (Sep-25 lcov, **two days stale** — 16 measured
files have changed and `coverage.db` records no commit):

| metric | recorded | uncovered | covered |
|---|---|---|---|
| lines | 27538 | 519 | 98.12% |
| branches | 3912 | 333 | 91.49% |
| functions | 2928 | 113 | **96.14%** (was reported 59.57%) |

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-27) — sash-convert no longer passes bad input silently ══

**A conversion downgrade the user was never told about.** tree-sitter-bash
0.25 cannot parse a glued `=` inside single brackets: `[ a=b ]` reads as an
assignment prefix plus a command named `]`, so no `test_command` node exists,
`convert_test_command` never runs, and the text is emitted verbatim. That
output then **compiles** — sash has no `[` builtin, so DD#23 resolves `[` to
the external `/usr/bin/[`. A bash test became a forked coreutils invocation
with nothing said. Nothing unsound (the manifest discloses the external), but
a downgrade has to be disclosed rather than inferred.

`convert.rs`'s `ERROR` arm handled exactly one grammar hole (`${a[a[0]]}`,
DD#80) and fell through silently for everything else. It now emits
`# MANUAL: could not parse …` for any ERROR it does not recognise.

Two details beyond the one-liner: **only the outermost ERROR is reported**
(tree-sitter fragments a bad region into nested ERRORs — the inner spans are
artefacts of the failed parse), and **the guard suppresses the note, not the
recursion**, so a recognisable construct nested deeper inside a bad span is
still rewritten.

Journal 427. Gate: predicted 6581, swept 6581, zero failing, zero flips, 5 new
ids (`57.173`-`57.177`, native-only — `convert.sh` does not run in c mode).
Controls: `57.174` (same test without the glued `=` converts and is NOT
reported) and `57.176` (the DD#80 ERROR is still recognised and unreported,
pinning that the generic note did not swallow the specific handler). `57.175`
**counts** the notes, the only form that detects the nested duplicate.

The `[ a=b ]`-specific rewrite was deliberately not done — the task made it
conditional on the generic warning proving noisy, and the whole suite produced
zero new notes.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-27) — DD#120: the invoker's channel ══

**A redirect written on a command is a channel for that command's output, and
never captures the invoker's.** DG's framing: "the setup belongs to the
program invoking cmd, and is not intended to consume the output of the
invoker." Every diagnostic sash emits is the invoker speaking about its own
failure — setup failure, exec failure, the DD#55 status abort, attest,
arithmetic aborts — so none of them can land in `cmd 2> f`. To capture them,
redirect the invoker: `exec 2>> errlog`.

This is a **deliberate divergence from every POSIX shell** (bash, dash and
busybox all route these through the already-applied redirects). That
behaviour is emergent, not designed — the tell is that `cmd 2>capt >bad` and
`cmd >bad 2>capt` put the message in different files. Under DD#120 the order
dependence disappears.

**Mechanism: one object, not a rule at twelve emit sites.** The runtime holds
`SASH_SCOPE_SAVE` — the invoker's own 0/1/2, `F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC` copies taken in
`sash_startup` (which both backends reach via `_start`, so neither needed a
prologue change). `sash_scope_bind()` re-takes them after a persistent `exec`
redirect; `sash_scope_restore()` puts them back on entry to END. CLOEXEC is
load-bearing: the fd survives a *failed* `execve` so the child can report, and
vanishes on a successful one.

**It also fixed a live bug in both backends.** `END { echo cleanup }` after
`/bin/false > out.txt` wrote `cleanup` **into `out.txt`** — the abort
terminates the block before the command's restore, stranding it on an
unreachable edge. Three abort paths leaked (status, exec failure, echo write
failure); only setup failure was safe, and only by accident. DG's question —
"if the diag fd exists, why does END need anything else?" — is what turned a
fd-2 diagnostic channel into the 0/1/2 scope set that fixes all three at
once, rather than a per-site restore rule that this bug proves gets
forgotten.

Journal 426. Gate: predicted 6576, swept 6576, zero failing, zero flips, 18
new ids (`iv.1`-`iv.9` × 2 modes); `rd.5`/`rd.7`/`rd.8` rewritten to the new
model. Every new check is paired with a control — `iv.3` (a running command's
stderr still reaches the redirect), `iv.5` (same diagnostic, same fd, only
the scope differs) and `iv.9` (END follows a persistent `exec >`, so the
restore is a restore and not a reset to the startup fds).

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-27) — redirect diagnostic fixed in BOTH backends ══

**A bug the differential oracle was structurally unable to see.** DD#55's
redirect setup-failure diagnostic must be written through the redirects that
already succeeded — bash puts `cmd 2> capt.txt > /bad`'s message *in*
`capt.txt`. native wrote it after `emit_restore`, so it went to the terminal.

Fixing that turned up **a second copy of the same inversion in the C
backend**, on the function-redirect scope path (`emit_redirect_push`). C's
`emit_redirect_guarded_body` had the order right, so `emit_c.rs` held two
functions doing one job in opposite orders — and the wrong one was paired
against a native function that was also wrong.

**That is why it survived: the oracle compares the backends to each other.**
Two identical wrong answers look exactly like two right ones. The command
form was caught (journal 404) because the backends *disagreed*; the scope
form, one line away, did not. The oracle localises a bug to one backend; it
cannot see a bug in the specification both were written from. Only bash can,
and only when someone writes the differential by hand.

Fix: `emit_open_failure_abort` split into `emit_open_failure_msg` +
`emit_open_failure_terminate`, with `emit_restore` between them — the three
functions had been one, which is why the restore could not simply be moved.

Specs `rd.5`-`rd.8` (`errors.sh`). `rd.6` is the ordering control that makes
`rd.5` mean anything. Neuter is diagnostic, not just non-vacuous: the native
inversion fails rd.5/rd.7/rd.8, the C inversion fails **rd.7 only**.

Not a bug, checked first: silence for a failure caught by `if`/`&&`/`||` is
DD#55 (55.25/55.50).

**Next up:** `convert-silent-passthrough-on-parse-error` (P2) — sash-convert
emits unparseable input verbatim with no `# MANUAL:` note, so a bash `[ a=b ]`
silently becomes a forked `/usr/bin/[` instead of a `[[ ]]`.

Gate: predicted 6558, swept 6558, zero failing, zero flips, eight new ids.
`mk test` 107/0. Clippy clean.

## ══ PREVIOUS (2026-09-26) — one command-substitution parser, not two ══

**The P1 wildcard audit found its first bug one layer up, in the parser.**
A double-quoted string had its **own** command-substitution parser. It had
drifted from the real one in the two ways two implementations of one thing
always drift, and both were user-reachable:

- **No `<` probe.** `"$(<f)"` became a command substitution with an *empty
  body*, so `echo "$(</etc/hostname)"` printed nothing where bash prints
  the file.
- **No way to carry a diagnostic.** Declared `-> Vec<Statement>`, it ended
  `Err(_) => break`. `parse_statement` reported the error correctly every
  time; the caller discarded it. `"$(if)"` compiled silently and
  `"$(echo a; if)"` compiled, exited 0, and dropped its tail.

**The taint bypass is the part that matters.** Unquoted `$(<f)` is SB5020 —
file contents are external input. With an empty body there was nothing to
taint, so `str v="$(<f)"` laundered tainted content into a clean-looking
variable. Two quote characters, straight through the taint model.

**DG settled it by principle, not by case:** interpolation and concatenation
of tainted content both model as a read, and a read of a tainted value can
only happen in `attest`. So a quoted slurp is a real `SlurpFile`, tainted,
identical to the unquoted spelling — and the fix is to stop maintaining a
second parser (option C), not to patch two symptoms. `command_sub_to_expr`
now delegates to `parse_command_substitution`; `parse_sub_script` is gone.
The precedent was already in the same file: the `ArithSub` arm beside the
call site was fixed for the identical bug in `$(( ))`.

**`cov.205` was covering nothing and had to go.** It asserted that
`"$(int x=1)"` compiles clean, on the stated grounds that the quoted path
reached a guard the unquoted one did not. The quoted path had no such probe
at all, and the clean compile it pinned *was the swallowed parse error*. A
spec whose passing depends on a bug converts the bug into something the
suite defends. Replaced with a body that reaches the guard structurally

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-26) — `$$` is punctuation sugar ══

**The magic-variable directive has started, `$$` first.** DD#111 §Why already
states the rule — *"Variables are not magic in sash… `$?` is punctuation sugar
for the `status` intrinsic. The intrinsic is the real thing."* — and the
compiler believed the opposite: the parser **folded** `$(getpid)` into a
`SimpleExpansion("$")`. The sugar was the real thing and the intrinsic
collapsed into it. That direction is now reversed for `$$`.

**I was wrong to offer DG a "defer" option** and said so. DD#111 is a stated
design rule, so step 1 of the decision tree applies (settled by a source of
truth) and applies to all three magic variables. The genuine forks were only
mechanism and sequencing; DG ruled **B + assertion**, **unify = true**,
**incremental**.

**DD#119 had already cleared the road.** Its "How it started" records the
*previous* attempt at this desugar and the blocker that killed it
(`> $$` tripping SB4049); DD#119 removed that blocker three commits ago, and
line 60 lists intrinsics as valid redirect targets.

**A typing bug fixed structurally.** `int a=$(getpid)` compiled; `int b=$$`
was SB4030 "cannot assign string value to int variable" — two spellings of one
value with two types, identical in kind to the `$!` bug `a875d58` patched by
seeding `intrinsic_int`. After the desugar there is no `$$` node left to
mistype. Deliberate consequence: `str c=$$` now rejects and directs you to
quote it; `str d="$$"` works. Same migration `cov.252b` took in `a875d58`;
`cov.252a` takes it here.

**One table, because they had already drifted.** `resolve_nullary_sexpr` knew
`getpid`→`$`/`status`→`?`/`getcpid`→`!` but only on the arith sexpr path; the
word form reached the same slot via the parser fold. Now
`magic_intrinsic_var`, read by both. Swept **in isolation** first (6510, zero
failing) so the next sweep's diff was attributable.

**The assertion is what makes option B safe.** `parse()` ends with
`assert_no_magic_sugar`, which ICEs on any surviving `SimpleExpansion` of
`$`/`?`/`!`. Four of eight construction sites can receive a magic name and all
four are routed; the other four are excluded **by construction**, not by
inspection.

**The flip check was vacuous — flagged to DG, not patched.** AGENTS.md's
regression recipe picks the baseline with `MAX(rowid)` at a `commit_hash`.
With a dirty tree, three sweeps shared `cc0b7a9`, so it selected *this* run
and compared it to itself — zero flips, and it could not have reported
anything else. The tell was 19538 rows at one hash (6510 + 6510 + 6518).
Re-run rowid-bounded it passes honestly. **A gate that cannot fail is not a
gate**; the recipe lives in AGENTS.md and the fix is DG's call.

Sweep **6518** — predicted exactly (6510 + 4 dual-mode specs). Zero failing,
zero retirements; vs the first `cc0b7a9` sweep: 0 flips, 8 new, 0 gone.
`mk test` and clippy clean. Both mechanisms neuter-proved; `spv.7` survives
the desugar neuter and is **labelled in place as a non-proof**. Journal 419.

**Next, in DG's order:**

1. **`$!` → `$(getcpid)`** — add the `"!"` arm to `magic_sugar_expansion`;
   delete the `getcpid` arm of `bareword_shortcut_expansion` and
   `parse_getcpid_word`'s `SpecialWord::Returned` fold. Lower risk.
2. **`$?` → `$(status)`** — the largest step, and it carries the trap:

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-26) — `-t` is retired ══

**DG's call: `-t` ceases to be a `[[ ]]` test.** It joins `-v`, `-o` and `-R`
in `unsupported_unary_test_hint` — SB5028 at validate. `-t` **stays** in the
parser's `is_unary_test_op`, deliberately: drop it there and `[[ -t 1 ]]`
degrades into two words and reports SB4014 instead. Parser permissive,
validate authoritative.

It was the odd one out on a real axis. The `[[ ]]` unary family is string
shape (`-n`/`-z`) and file predicates; every one takes a string. `-t` took an
**fd number** — the sole int-typed unary test — and `emit_isatty_test` was the
only unary arm that had to `atoi` its operand first. It also asks an
interactivity question, which a compiled static binary has little business
asking.

**`terminal?` is dropped as YAGNI (DG).** Supporting fact: sash arithmetic has
**no** unary predicates at all (`IrUnaryArithOp` = Neg/Pos/Not/BitNot; only
`!` is a predicate; every sexpr intrinsic is value-producing), so it would
have been the first of its kind — in a language whose predicate context
(`[[ ]]`) it would have been declining to use.

**The removal is total**, down through both backends and the runtime: the
`tests.rs` dispatch arm and `emit_isatty_test`, the `setup.rs` extern
declaration, `ExternFuncs::isatty`, the `emit_c.rs` arm and its
`extern i64 sash_isatty(i64)`, and `sash_isatty` itself in `sash-rt`. rustc
found the edge: deleting the dispatch arm left `atoi_call` unused in
`tests.rs`, which is "it was the only int-typed test" arriving from the other
direction.

**The neuter proved a long-standing claim.** `unsupported_unary_test_hint`'s
doc comment has said these operators "must be rejected here (SB5028) before
codegen ICEs on them". Neutering the `-t` arm ICEs at `tests.rs:194`. First
demonstration; the claim was true.

`cov.89` retires with the mechanism it covered — predicted, and the sweep
announced exactly `c:cov.89` / `native:cov.89`. Net spec count unchanged
(one dual-mode out, one in: `62.22`), so the purge naming those two ids was
the sharp prediction rather than the total.

Sweep **6510** (native 3355, c 3142, skipped 13) — predicted exactly. Zero
failing, zero flips vs `a875d58`. `mk test` exit 0. Journal 418.

**DD#89 is closed** (same commit batch): its "Left open" section asked whether
`exit $s` / `return $s` should reject, and all five tracked sites now do —
**every one by rejection, none by coercion**. `$(arg $s)` was the most

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-26) — exit, wait and arg take a number ══

**DG's int-only directive is in.** `exit`, `wait` and `arg` accept int-type
only, via one shared check that is the exact mirror of
`check_string_intrinsic_operands` (that one rejects an int where a string is
required).

`arg` was the worst by a distance: `$(arg $s)` on a string silently yielded
**argv[0]** — no diagnostic, no trace. `exit $s` / `wait $s` coerced through
atoi to 0, a defensible wrong answer by comparison.

DG's three calls: **`exit ''''''` is rejected** (it read as 0, i.e. *success*, for a
script that meant to fail); **a quoted number is a string**, so `exit "1"` is
rejected — quoting is the int→string conversion everywhere else in sash and
cannot mean the opposite here; **signed literals stay legal**, `exit -1` → 255.
`$(( ${s:?bad} ))` is the accountable conversion and is strictly better than
the atoi it replaces: it aborts with the author'''s message instead of quietly
reporting success. Only slot 0 is a sink — `arg N default` keeps its string
default (isink.10).

**`$!` is now int-typed.** `wait $!` is *the* idiom and it broke: `$!` was
String while `$(getcpid)`, which `$!` is sugar for, was already int-returning.
`intrinsic_int` seeded `?` but not `!`, so `wait $(getcpid)` would have passed
a rule `wait $!` failed — two spellings of one value. The asymmetry was the
bug. It is also a step toward the parked magic-variable directive, and it is
what exposed the C renderer bug fixed in `b251d75`.

**The sequencing was DG'''s call and it mattered.** `arg` is only ever written
as `$(arg …)`, an expression — so wired the old way this check would have
caught `echo $(arg $s)` and missed `str t=$(arg $s)`, leaving the exact case
the directive exists to close open behind a green spec. Fixing the traversal
first, in its own commit (`6013848`), is why this change is small.

Sweep **6510** (native 3355, c 3142, skipped 13) = predicted exactly. Zero
failing, zero flips vs `b251d75`. Non-vacuity proved twice: neutering the
check fails the 5 rejection specs and leaves all 7 positives green; neutering
the `$!` seed alone fails 3 specs across two files.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-26) — a target must prove itself ══

**DD#119 is in: a redirect target must be provably non-empty, and
string-typed.** This came out of the magic-variable directive rather than
being aimed at redirects. Desugaring `$$` to `$(getpid)` broke `> $$`, because
the target became a `CommandSubstitution` and SB4049 rejects those at parse.
I offered DG four options; he took none of them and asked instead what if a
redirect target had to carry a disposition. That attacks the **actual** bug
class — `bug-redirect-nonsimple-target-empty` was an *empty* filename, not a
complicated one — and needs no carve-out and no `ExprKind::Intrinsic` node.

Dispositions are the *proof mechanism*, but the rule tests **"does the result
prove non-empty"**, not "did you write a disposition". That distinction is
load-bearing: the looser wording would admit `${p:~}` and `${p:-}` and let the
original bug back in wearing the remedy's clothes.

DG settled three details: **array cells are in** (a cell behaves like a string
variable), **concat is strict** (`> $p.log` with empty `p` silently writes a
hidden `.log`), and ints are **exempt but still need quotes** — quoting is how
int becomes string everywhere else in sash.

**Three bugs found and fixed**, none related to each other:

- A **native ICE from ordinary source** — `int p=5; ... > $p.log`, three
  shapes. `redirect_expr_simple_expansion` called `str_ptr()` unconditionally;
  braced spellings survived only because the transform spills `${p}` targets
  to a scalar temp. The comment at `types.rs:19` *claimed* unreachability and
  listed its audited callers — `redirects.rs` was not among them. Corrected.
- A **missing C `Concat` arm** in `ir_expr_as_str`.
- Behind it, a **silent wrong answer**: `latest_var_as_str` returned `""` for
  int vars, deferred in a comment as "rare enough". Not an ICE — just quietly
  wrong. It surfaced **only** because native 14.59 passed and c:14.59 failed,
  which is exactly the differential oracle's job.

Sweep **6464** (native 3332, c 3119, skipped 13) — the predicted total
exactly. Zero failing, zero flips vs `505b581`; `mk test` 59/27/20.
Non-vacuity took **three** neuters, one per mechanism, each failing exactly
its own cohort (6 / 1 / 1).

**One wart, recorded in the DD rather than papered over:** `lib.rs:387` prints
every `TypeError` as SB4030, so all of DD#119's rejections share that code.
The int exemption needs `env.var_type`, which pins the rule to

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-25) — the key is a type, not a spelling ══

**The strict subscript rules are in.** An array index must be int-typed; a
map key must not be. Both surfaces enforce the same rule, which journal 413
made possible by giving the assignment LHS the read side's index grammar.

The predicate that stood there asked the *negative* question — "is this a
string key" — and could only name the forms it knew. `var_type` ends in
`unwrap_or(String)`, so "declared a string" and "never recorded" are the same
answer and no such test can separate them. It now asks for `Int` and
delegates the typing to `expr_type`, inheriting DD#76's int-array cell,
`Arithmetic => Int`, and the rule that a `:-`/`:?` disposition keeps its
*subject's* type — so a bare disposition on a string is rejected and one on
an int is not, without either case being written here.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-25) — the left side that could not say it ══

**The assignment LHS now accepts every subscript index the read side does.**
DG's directive after the DD#80 work: enforce the strictest forms — array
indexes must be integers, map keys strings — and **"assignment and read should
be uniform in what they accept."** The uniformity clause had to come first,
because the write side was a strictly narrower surface and could not host the
rules.

Measured before: `${a[$(( … ))]}` read fine, `a[$(( … ))]=` was SB5011;
`${a[${s:-2}]}` read fine, `a[${s:-2}]=` was SB4014; `${m["$i"]}` read fine,
`m["$i"]=` was SB4014. **`$(( … ))` is the conversion DD#80 itself names as
the remedy for a string index**, and it was unusable on the left of an `=` —
so an author told to convert had nowhere to put the conversion. The two
failures did not even agree on a code: one reached the parser (SB4014), the
other never looked like an assignment, so `a[` became a command name and the
error was *command not found* for a typed-index problem.

`parse_split_subscript_index` took exactly one token — `Tok::Dollar` or a
`DollarBrace` holding a bare identifier — because the shape probe pinned the
index at `peek_n(2) == "]"`. The fix recovers the raw index text from the
token spans and hands it to **`expr::parse_subscript_index`, the same function
the read path calls**. One list of accepted forms, both sides call it; the
parity is now structural rather than two lists kept in step by hand.

Three existing specs changed, all improvements: `a[ x ]=5` now reports the
real fault (SB4030, string key on an array) instead of SB5011; `m[${k:-z}]=1`
is honoured; and `m[${#k}]=1` reports SB4038, the `${#…}` retirement — the
same message the read side gives for the same text. The LHS did not learn
about `${#…}`; it stopped having an opinion of its own.

## ══ STATUS (2026-09-25) — the type that was only half known ══

**A `str`-declared scalar no longer silently indexes an array at 0.** DG:
"no string subscript for arrays." `str s=abc; ${a[$s]}` printed element 0;
`a[$s]=99` wrote it. The bareword `${a[s]}`, the quoted `${a["abc"]}` and the
arithmetic `(( a[s] ))` all rejected — same array, same variable, two answers
by spelling. Read, write and append close together: `check_assignment` and
`check_subscript_types` share `check_subscript_key_kind`.

**The framing I filed it under was an over-read, and the sweep caught it.**
DD#80 uses "string key" structurally — "a clean bareword or a quoted string" —
not "a variable whose type is string". `$var` is a separate enumerated form
with no type proviso. Rejecting every string-*typed* index cost **8 specs in
both modes**, including two the DDs bless: `attest i i?` (60.70, DD#93's
"documented way through") and `${arr[$1]}` (80.31, "Bash agrees").

The mechanism is one line — `var_type` ends in `unwrap_or(VarType::String)`,
so **"declared a string" and "never recorded" are the same answer**, and a
bare `i=1` records `String` exactly like `str s=abc` (sash types a bare
numeric literal as a string, per bash). So the shipped rule is narrow: a new
`declared_str` set, rejecting only a *positively declared* `str`. The old
`// could be either` comment was right about every case except the one it
could have decided.

**The map side is not a mirror bug.** `${m[0]}` rejects, `int i=0; ${m[$i]}`
does not — the same literal-only shape. DD#80: "any string is a valid key",
and DD#33's bare-integer rejection is anti-ambiguity ("it reads like an array
index"), not a type rule. Checking `notes/decisions/` first stopped that fix.

**A second find, caught by checking a sentence I had already written.** Because
read and write share the check, the write path inherited the read path's advice
— and `a[${s:?m}]=Q` does **not** parse (SB4014; DD#33's LHS takes a bare
`$var` only). The rejection pointed into a wall. The message is now
surface-specific: the read path names the disposition, the write path names an
`int` variable or converting first (`int i=$(( ${s:-2} )); a[$i]=…`). Specs
80.49/80.50 pin it. Lifting the DD#33 LHS restriction is filed, not done.

The SB4030 text for a variable index also stopped recommending `${a[$i]}`,
which sent an author from one SB4030 to the same one.
